rows.statement: Experiment 21: a component with disabled deployment is potentially Deprecated/Inactive, not an ActiveRuntimeComponent; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 111.48 — Component ownership ... Owner(C). Possible owners: team, product, architecture domain, platform, external provider.
rows.statement: Defines Owner(C) with five possible owner categories: team, product, architecture domain, platform, external provider.

rows.anchor: 111.49 — Experiment 22 ... No owner can be established. Expected: Owner=Unknown. This is itself an architectural governance finding. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: an unestablishable owner yields Owner=Unknown, itself an architectural governance finding; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 111.50 — Component criticality ... Criticality(C)∈{Critical,High,Medium,Low}. Based on impact, not code size.
rows.statement: Defines Criticality(C)∈{Critical,High,Medium,Low} based on impact rather than code size.

rows.anchor: 111.51 — Experiment 23 ... A 50-line authorization service controls production changes. Expected: potentially Critical. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: a small 50-line authorization service controlling production changes is potentially Critical despite its size; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 111.52 — Test coverage ... Verification(C) should identify unit tests, integration tests, architecture tests, security tests, runtime tests.
rows.statement: Defines per-component Verification(C) identifying unit/integration/architecture/security/runtime tests.

rows.anchor: 111.53 — Experiment 24 ... Critical governance component has no automated tests. Expected: AssuranceGap. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: a critical governance component with no automated tests is an AssuranceGap; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 111.54 — Component evidence card ... COMPONENT: X with Logical role, Observed responsibility, Owns, Reads, Writes, Inbound, Outbound, Dependencies, Rules, Tests, Runtime, Owner, Architecture mapping, Evidence, Confidence, Conformance. This becomes the atomic unit of reconstruction.
rows.statement: Specifies the 16-field Component Evidence Card schema as the atomic unit of reconstruction.

rows.anchor: 111.55 — Component relationship graph ... G_C=(Components,Relationships). Calls, Reads, Writes, Publishes, Subscribes, Implements, Verifies, Owns.
rows.statement: Defines the component relationship graph G_C=(Components,Relationships) with eight relationship types.

rows.anchor: 111.56 — Experiment 25 ... Two components share a database. Graph records A-writes->DB, B-writes->DB. Expected: potential ownership conflict becomes visible. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: two components both writing to a shared database surfaces a potential ownership conflict via the relationship graph; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 111.57 — Architecture smell detection ... Hub component, Circular dependency, Shared database coupling, Orphan, Duplicate capability. These are signals, not automatic violations.
rows.statement: Defines five architecture-smell patterns detectable from the component graph (Hub, Circular dependency, Shared database coupling, Orphan, Duplicate capability), explicitly framed as signals rather than automatic violations.

rows.statement: Experiment 26: a graph cycle A→B→C→A is flagged CircularDependencyCandidate; result PASS.

rows.statement: Defines agent-component relationship mapping: Claude/Codex to KnowledgeOS, Agent to Repository/Verification/Evidence.

rows.statement: Experiment 27: Claude modifying the repository while bypassing KnowledgeOS governance is a potential agent governance boundary violation, classified OBS/DRIFT depending on intended workflow.

rows.anchor: 111.61 — Shared infrastructure ... If Claude and Codex share VerificationEngine, that is useful evidence of a common assurance layer.
rows.statement: States a shared VerificationEngine between Claude and Codex is useful evidence of a common assurance layer.

rows.anchor: 111.62 — Experiment 28 ... Claude has one verification mechanism. Codex has another incompatible verification mechanism. Expected: potential assurance fragmentation. Result: OBS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: incompatible per-agent verification mechanisms (Claude vs Codex) is potential assurance fragmentation, classified OBS.

rows.anchor: 111.63 — The ideal agent relationship ... KnowledgeOS with Common Rules, Common Evidence, Common Governance shared by Claude and Codex. Not Claude→private architecture, Codex→private architecture.
rows.statement: Presents the ideal shared-infrastructure diagram (KnowledgeOS with Common Rules/Evidence/Governance shared by Claude and Codex), contrasted with the undesired private-per-agent-architecture pattern.

rows.anchor: 111.64 — Component inventory status model ... Status∈{Confirmed,Candidate,Legacy,External,Duplicate,Overlapping,Unknown}. This avoids premature architecture decisions.
rows.statement: Defines a seven-value component inventory status model (Confirmed/Candidate/Legacy/External/Duplicate/Overlapping/Unknown), avoiding premature architecture decisions.

rows.anchor: 111.65 — Experiment 29 ... Two components appear to implement the same capability. Expected: DuplicateCandidate. Not immediately DeleteOne. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: two apparently-duplicate components are classified DuplicateCandidate, not immediately marked for deletion; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 111.66 — Reconstruction confidence ... Confidence(C)=f(Structure,Source,Tests,Deployment,Runtime). High: Source+Tests+Runtime. Medium: Source+Tests. Low: DocumentationOnly.

rows.statement: Presents an illustrative actual component map (KnowledgeOS->Knowledge/Governance/Assurance->nine components C1-C9) with labels required to come from actual repository evidence, not invention.

rows.anchor: 111.68 — The important discovery criterion ... The most important output is not the number of components. It is whether the component graph exhibits CoherentBoundaries. We want to discover whether Responsibility→Data→Behavior→Ownership aligns.
rows.statement: States the central discovery criterion CoherentBoundaries: whether Responsibility->Data->Behavior->Ownership align, more important than component count.

rows.anchor: 111.69 — The key diagnostic ... Outcome A Coherent (Components≈ArchitecturalBoundaries). Outcome B Fragmented (OneConcept→ManyOverlappingComponents). Outcome C Monolithic (ManyConcepts→OneLargeComponent). These lead to very different architectural conclusions.
rows.statement: Defines three mutually exclusive architectural outcomes -- Coherent, Fragmented, Monolithic -- each stated to lead to materially different architectural conclusions.

rows.statement: Experiment 30: evidence/governance/agent-control/runtime-assurance sharing one monolithic service and tables is a potential MonolithicKnowledgeOSCore, classified OBS and explicitly not automatically wrong but materially different from a distributed architecture.

rows.statement: Defines the converse ArchitectureFragmentation outcome, illustrated by Evidence spanning four unrelated implementations and Governance spanning three different mechanisms.

rows.anchor: 111.72 — What we should not do yet ... We should not redesign anything. We should not conclude 'This service must be split.' We should first establish ObservedArchitecture. Then TargetArchitecture. Then Gap. Only afterward Remediation.
rows.statement: States a strict anti-premature-redesign discipline: ObservedArchitecture->TargetArchitecture->Gap->Remediation in that order, never jumping to a redesign conclusion.

rows.anchor: 111.73 — Step 111 verdict ... The actual component inventory methodology is now defined: Repository→Component→Responsibility→Data→Interface→Dependency→Verification→Runtime. The next empirical artifact is KnowledgeOS Actual Component Inventory with evidence attached to every significant claim.
rows.statement: Records the Step 111 methodology pipeline Repository->Component->Responsibility->Data->Interface->Dependency->Verification->Runtime, naming the KnowledgeOS Actual Component Inventory as the next empirical artifact.

aliases: Information Acquisition, Value of Information, Active Learning and the Next-Best Epistemic Action

sources.note: S0927's Step 34: the fully worked EVPI/EVSI/NVOI-based Next-Best-Epistemic-Action formalization, generalizing active learning beyond ML; extends decision-theory-value-of-information-algebra (S0910/Step 25R) with decision-boundary uncertainty, epistemic-action taxonomy, and the value-of-contradiction/disconfirmation-seeking principle. This file's own text places it after a not-yet-processed Step 33, confirming this batch's step-number deviation pattern.

rows.anchor: Inference asks what can we conclude from what we know. Step 34 asks What should we learn next? ... a fundamentally different problem
rows.statement: Distinguishes inference from information-acquisition selection as fundamentally different problems.

rows.anchor: 10^6 uncertain assertions ... impossible and unnecessary to validate all of them immediately ... Choose the information acquisition action that produces the greatest useful improvement relative to its cost
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS should not investigate everything, requiring a cost-relative optimization.

rows.anchor: QueryCMDB, InspectRuntime, AskDomainExpert, RunTest, PerformExperiment, RetrieveDocument, CompareIndependentSource ... produces an observation Y_I
rows.statement: Defines the information-gathering action set with seven worked examples.

rows.anchor: Cost(I) ... Time, Money, Compute, HumanAttention, OperationalRisk ... information is not free
rows.statement: Defines Cost(I) across five components.

rows.anchor: EVPI=L_0-L_{PI} ... an upper bound on the value of information
rows.statement: Formally defines Expected Value of Perfect Information as an upper bound.

rows.anchor: EVSI(I)=L_0-E_Y[\min_d E[L(d,\theta)\mid K,Y]] ... NVOI(I)=EVSI(I)-Cost(I) ... the core mathematical idea
rows.statement: Formally defines Expected Value of Sample Information and net value of information as the step's core idea.

rows.anchor: I^*=\arg\max_{I\in\mathcal I}NVOI(I) ... our first formal definition of NextBestEpistemicAction
rows.statement: Defines the first formal Next-Best-Epistemic-Action.

rows.anchor: InformationValue\neq UncertaintyReduction ... A has no influence on any important decision ... UncertaintyReduction(A) may have almost zero practical value
rows.statement: States the subtle principle that information value is not the same as uncertainty reduction.

rows.anchor: DecisionSensitivity(A,D) ... Information about A is valuable if learning A can change d^*
rows.statement: Defines DecisionSensitivity as the criterion for information value.

rows.anchor: Nexus has 31 GB RAM ... migration architecture does not depend on RAM beyond a very large safety margin ... almost no decision value
rows.statement: Worked example of low-decision-sensitivity uncertainty (RAM precision beyond safety margin).

rows.anchor: Production database backup is restorable ... DecisionSensitivity(B,D) is very high ... validating B may have extremely high VOI
rows.statement: Worked contrasting example of high-decision-sensitivity uncertainty (backup restorability).

rows.anchor: d^*=f(K) ... If perturbing A does not change f(K), then A has low local decision sensitivity
rows.statement: Formalizes a decision-relevance partition via perturbation of the decision function.

rows.anchor: Closure(A) ... A\rightarrow B\rightarrow D ... DependencyClosure+DecisionCriticality=EpistemicPrioritization
rows.statement: Combines Step 32's dependency closure with decision dependency, giving a prioritization formula.

rows.anchor: Criticality(D) ... Low, Medium, High, Critical ... should be domain-owned. KnowledgeOS can consume it but should not invent the business meaning
rows.statement: Defines a domain-owned Criticality classification, not invented by KnowledgeOS.

rows.anchor: EL(d)=E[L(d,\theta)\mid K] ... d^*=\arg\min_d EL(d) ... d_1 expected loss 10, d_2 expected loss 12 ... investigation may reveal a high-risk state in which d_2 becomes preferable
rows.statement: Defines expected loss and current-optimal decision, worked with a two-decision expected-loss-reversal example.

rows.anchor: Risk<5\%\Rightarrow AutomaticApproval ... Risk\in[3\%,8\%] ... DecisionBoundaryUncertainty. Uncertainty far from a decision boundary may be harmless. Uncertainty near a boundary can be critical
rows.statement: Introduces DecisionBoundaryUncertainty, worked with a threshold-straddling risk-interval example.

rows.anchor: Risk\in[1\%,2\%] ... no urgent investigation ... Risk\in[4\%,7\%] crosses the decision boundary ... additional evidence is valuable
rows.statement: Worked contrasting examples of harmless-far and critical-boundary-straddling risk intervals.

rows.anchor: Priority(A)\propto DecisionImpact(A)\times Uncertainty(A) ... conceptual, not yet a universal formula
rows.statement: Proposes a conceptual, not-yet-universal epistemic-triage priority formula.

rows.anchor: EVSI(I)=10, Cost(I)=2, NVOI(I)=8 ... EVSI=12, Cost=20, NVOI=-8 ... should not be prioritized merely because it provides more information
rows.statement: Worked arithmetic example showing higher-EVSI investigations can have lower net value once cost is subtracted.

rows.anchor: HumanAttention is an epistemic resource ... 2 hours of a senior architect's time may be more expensive than a machine-readable check
rows.statement: States human attention is itself a costed epistemic resource, worked with a comparison example.

rows.anchor: 1000 CPU hours ... 5 seconds ... Even if both reduce uncertainty, their priorities differ
rows.statement: Notes compute cost differences between validations matter even for similar uncertainty reduction.

rows.anchor: ProductionInspection may be more dangerous than ReadOnlyMetadataQuery ... Cost(I) should include OperationalRisk
rows.statement: Requires Cost(I) to include operational risk, worked with a contrasting example.

rows.anchor: Existing evidence -> Existing independent evidence -> Read-only observation -> Automated validation -> Simulation -> Controlled experiment -> Expert investigation -> Operational intervention
rows.statement: Presents an eight-stage information-acquisition preference hierarchy, exact ordering cost/risk-dependent.

rows.anchor: SearchExistingEvidence ... If sufficient evidence already exists, NewInvestigation has low or zero additional value ... prevents unnecessary work
rows.statement: Requires reusing existing evidence before new investigation.

rows.anchor: Sufficient(E,A,D) ... EvidenceSufficiency is decision-relative
rows.statement: Defines decision-relative evidence sufficiency.

rows.anchor: A screenshot may be sufficient to answer Is the application running? but insufficient to answer Is the application production-ready?
rows.statement: Worked example illustrating decision-relative sufficiency.

rows.anchor: ActiveLearning ... a model selects the next observation most useful for improving itself ... KnowledgeOS can generalize this idea beyond ML
rows.statement: Introduces active learning and generalizes it beyond machine learning to epistemic active learning.

rows.anchor: IG(Q)=H(K)-E[H(K\mid Q)] ... InformationGain\neq DecisionValue
rows.statement: Defines entropy-based information gain and states InformationGain ≠ DecisionValue.

rows.anchor: DWIG(Q)=DecisionImpact(Q)\times IG(Q) ... not a universal law, but it illustrates the correct direction
rows.statement: Proposes decision-weighted information gain, explicitly not a universal law.

rows.anchor: Entropy treats all uncertainty reduction equally ... KnowledgeOS should therefore be decision-aware
rows.statement: Argues entropy-based measures fail to distinguish critical from irrelevant uncertainty reduction.

rows.anchor: What exactly does production-ready mean in this bounded context? ... Clarification is an information action
rows.statement: Introduces semantic clarification as its own first-class information action.

rows.anchor: Retrieve, Observe, Measure, Validate, Clarify, Experiment, Simulate, Ask, Compare, Recalculate
rows.statement: Defines a ten-value epistemic action-category taxonomy.

rows.anchor: SelectNext(K,D,\mathcal I)\rightarrow I^* ... must consider VOI, Cost, Risk, Dependency, Criticality
rows.statement: Defines an investigation-selection function considering five factors.

rows.anchor: ActionAuthority(I) ... ReadOnly, OperationallySensitive, HumanApprovalRequired ... Authorize(I,K) must be evaluated before execution
rows.statement: Requires an explicit action-authority gate before executing any selected information action, the same assurance principle as ordinary actions.

rows.anchor: Restart service to determine whether it recovers ... Experiment+Intervention. It requires a higher assurance level
rows.statement: Worked example distinguishing an information action that is really an intervention, requiring higher assurance.

rows.anchor: X\leftarrow Observe(W) [Observation] versus W\leftarrow do(X=x) [Intervention]. The second changes the world
rows.statement: Formally distinguishes observation from intervention as information-acquisition modes.

rows.anchor: Observational data may not identify causality. A controlled intervention do(X=x) may provide stronger evidence ... VOI_{causal} must include InterventionRisk
rows.statement: States controlled intervention can resolve causal ambiguity but its VOI must include intervention risk.

rows.anchor: I_1\rightarrow Observation\rightarrow I_2\rightarrow Observation... ... Policy: Y_1\rightarrow I_2 ... more efficient than deciding all investigations upfront
rows.statement: Defines sequential/adaptive information acquisition as a sequential decision problem.

rows.anchor: \pi:K_t\rightarrow I ... K_{t+1}=Update(K_t,Outcome_I) ... Assess\rightarrow Select\rightarrow Acquire\rightarrow Update\rightarrow Reassess
rows.statement: Formally defines an investigation policy closing into an epistemic control loop, substantially more powerful than a static repository.

rows.anchor: stop when NVOI(I)\le0 for all feasible investigations ... DecisionConfidence is sufficient under the applicable governance threshold. Not necessarily a single scalar confidence
rows.statement: Defines a stopping rule for the investigation process.

rows.anchor: SufficientKnowledgeForAction ... particularly important in real-world engineering
rows.statement: Introduces satisficing as the practical objective, rather than perfect knowledge.

rows.anchor: Sufficient(K,D) ... domain- and governance-aware
rows.statement: Defines a decision-sufficiency predicate.

rows.anchor: For low-criticality action, modest evidence ... For critical action, independent evidence; deterministic validation; explicit authorization; bounded uncertainty
rows.statement: Defines criticality-dependent sufficiency requirements.

rows.anchor: \sum_i Cost(I_i)\le B ... \max\sum_i Value(I_i) ... a resource-allocation problem
rows.statement: Defines a total investigation budget constraint with value maximization.

rows.anchor: Value(I_1,I_2)\neq Value(I_1)+Value(I_2) ... information complementarities and redundancies
rows.statement: States investigations can interact, giving non-additive combined value.

rows.anchor: I_1\approx I_2 ... their combined information value may be low ... provenance helps identify redundancy
rows.statement: Defines evidence redundancy identified via provenance.

rows.anchor: RuntimeInspection plus IndependentMonitoring ... materially increase epistemic strength
rows.statement: Worked example of genuinely independent investigations providing high combined value.

rows.anchor: An investigation can be valuable even if it increases uncertainty ... InformationValue can come from discovering that we are wrong
rows.statement: States the value-of-contradiction insight, worked with an example of a strongly-held belief challenged by an independent test.

rows.anchor: Find the cheapest high-quality evidence capable of changing my conclusion ... a much stronger epistemic strategy
rows.statement: Reframes the optimal investigation strategy as disconfirmation-seeking rather than confirmation-seeking.

rows.anchor: Priority(FalsificationTest) should often be high ... particularly when DecisionImpact and CurrentUncertainty are both high
rows.statement: States falsification-test priority should generally be high for high-impact, high-uncertainty critical claims.

rows.anchor: Experiments A-E: cheap-weak-redundant vs moderate-independent-decision-changing->NVOI(I2)>NVOI(I1) PASS; irrelevant-but-uncertain assertion->low priority PASS; moderately uncertain critical precondition->high priority PASS; entropy-reducing but decision-unchanging investigation->low decision value P
rows.statement: Runs a first group of five falsification tests (all PASS): a moderate-cost independent decision-changing investigation outranks a cheap weak redundant one; a highly-uncertain but decision-irrelevant assertion receives low priority; a moderately-uncertain critical precondition receives high priority; an entropy-reducing investigation that cannot change the decision has low decision value; and a cheap investigation determining whether an expensive one is needed is performed first.

experiment.hypothesis: The information-acquisition prioritization model correctly ranks investigations by net decision value rather than raw information gain or cost alone.
experiment.setup: Five scenarios comparing investigations by cost, independence, decision-relevance, and sequencing.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply the NVOI/DecisionSensitivity/DecisionBoundaryUncertainty rules to each scenario
experiment.result: All five scenarios produce the theoretically expected prioritization
experiment.interpretation: Confirms decision-relevance, not raw information content, drives prioritization.

rows.anchor: Experiments F-J: investigation could contradict high-confidence weakly-supported claim->potentially high priority PASS; operationally dangerous investigation->reduced priority, may require authorization PASS; privileged-access information action->authorization gate before execution PASS; investigati
rows.statement: Runs a second group of five falsification tests (all PASS): a potentially conclusion-contradicting investigation against a weakly-supported high-confidence claim receives potentially high priority; an operationally dangerous investigation has reduced priority and may require authorization; a privileged-access information action is gated by authorization before execution; an investigation revealing previously-unknown model uncertainty can still be classified as beneficial despite increasing measured uncertainty; and no feasible positive-net-value investigation yields StopInvestigation.

experiment.hypothesis: The model correctly prioritizes disconfirming evidence, gates risky/privileged investigations, tolerates uncertainty-increasing but beneficial investigations, and stops when no positive-value action remains.
experiment.setup: Five scenarios spanning disconfirmation value, operational risk, privileged access, uncertainty-increasing investigation, and investigation exhaustion.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply the disconfirmation/authorization/stopping rules to each scenario
experiment.result: All five scenarios produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: Confirms the model values disconfirmation and governs risky investigation appropriately.

rows.anchor: STEP 34 — PASS ... NextBestEpistemicAction ... I^*=\arg\max_I[EVSI(I)-Cost(I)] subject to Authorization, Safety, Resource, Governance constraints
rows.statement: Step 34 self-verdict: PASS, formalizing NextBestEpistemicAction subject to four governance constraints.

rows.anchor: Principle 1 Uncertainty reduction is not automatically valuable ... Principle 7 Information acquisition itself requires governance
rows.statement: Lists seven boxed architectural principles from Step 34.

rows.anchor: Knowledge Representation ... Knowledge Consistency ... Knowledge Validation ... Uncertainty Propagation ... Now Knowledge Acquisition ... becoming an active epistemic system
rows.statement: Restates the architectural progression, now including Knowledge Acquisition, becoming an active epistemic system.

rows.statement: Presents a consolidated thirteen-stage complete-loop restatement.

rows.anchor: finite epistemic budget across competing knowledge problems ... Portfolio-level epistemic resource optimization ... Step 35
rows.statement: Closes by posing the portfolio-level resource-allocation question across competing decisions/investigations, transitioning to Step 35 (Epistemic Resource Allocation, Attention Scheduling, Knowledge Triage, Portfolio Optimization), listing eight factors to combine, with the ultimate objective of maximizing organizational decision quality per unit of epistemic resource.

rows.statement: States epistemic uncertainty can be reduced by evidence, explicitly bridging to the Value-of-Information problem (Step 34).

rows.statement: Closes with a preview of Step 34 (Information Acquisition and Value of Information), duplicating -- in a shorter conceptual form -- the VOI/NextBestEpistemicAction content already fully extracted from S0927.

lineage_claims.quote: That will be the mathematical foundation of Step 34.

rows.statement: Formalizes a four-level optimization hierarchy spanning claim validation, investigation selection, decision-making, and portfolio-level allocation.

rows.anchor: How do we know that the entire epistemic system itself is behaving correctly over time? A model can be internally consistent and still systematically produce poor decisions ... Calibration, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, Coverage, False Discovery, False Assurance, Drift, Robustness. these metrics are
rows.statement: Closes by posing the meta-epistemology question of whether the epistemic system itself behaves correctly over time, listing nine candidate non-interchangeable meta-validation metrics and transitioning to Step 36 (Epistemic Calibration, Reliability, Meta-Validation and Knowledge-System Health): KnowledgeOS -> Evaluate(KnowledgeOS).

lineage_claims.quote: Step 36 — Epistemic Calibration, Reliability, Meta-Validation and Knowledge-System Health

rows.anchor: The same structure used for ValueOfInformation can be used after the fact to measure ActualInformationValue. This gives feedback to future prioritization

sources.note: Step 215's proposed (not executed) retrospective reconstruction methodology for Steps 1-182: a six-question per-step record, a 14-code step-type taxonomy crossed with F/D/P/U, a convergence test for independently-recurring principles, the 'distinction preservation' hypothesis (SemanticIntegrity proportional to DistinctionPreservation) unifying ten candidate A!=B distinctions, a chronology-first test for the Gita lens's actual historical role, a four-layer Observed/Intended/Implemented/Target architecture distinction, a 19-column Master Reconstruction Matrix schema, and a three-phase book-production architecture (Archaeology/Separation-of-Concerns/Synthesis).

rows.anchor: What happened? ... What remained unknown? ... R(S_i)=(O_i,L_i,A_i,V_i,U_i)
rows.statement: Defines a six-question per-step reconstruction record R(S_i)=(Observation,Learning,Architecture,Verification,Unknown) to be applied to each of Steps 1-182, explicitly changing mode from generating new theory to reconstructing the evidentiary basis of existing theory.

rows.anchor: StepCount ≠ KnowledgeCount ... exploratory; repetitive; corrective; validation; implementation; philosophical; mathematical; editorial; prompt-engineering; synthesis
rows.statement: States that a conversational 'step' is not necessarily an architectural contribution (some are exploratory, repetitive, corrective, editorial, etc.), so StepCount != KnowledgeCount, requiring the reconstruction to discover the actual knowledge-bearing events rather than treat all 182 steps as equal.

rows.anchor: OBS Observation ... UNK Insufficient evidence ... A single step can have more than one tag internally
rows.statement: Defines a 14-code step-type classification (OBS/EXP/MAT/DDD/ARC/GOV/AI/VER/FAIL/DEC/PHI/SYN/REP/UNK) allowing multiple tags per step, crossed with the F/D/P/U epistemic-status axis (Type x EpistemicStatus) so e.g. 'ARC+D' denotes an architectural derivation rather than an observed fact.

rows.anchor: Which architectural principles appear independently more than once? ... Convergence(I) = NumberOfIndependentEvidencePaths(I) ... We should not immediately turn this into a numerical quality score
rows.statement: Proposes a convergence test: if the same architectural principle emerges from multiple unrelated observations (P_1, P_7, P_31 all pointing to invariant I), that repeated independent emergence is treated as strong evidence the principle is fundamental, formalized as Convergence(I)=NumberOfIndependentEvidencePaths(I) but explicitly not reduced to a numerical quality score.

rows.anchor: Identity≠State ... Knowledge≠Authority ... Unknown≠False ... CurrentState≠History ... Generation≠Validation ... Validation≠Authorization ... Claim→Evidence ... Context_A≠Context_B ... These are candidate principles, not yet declared final conclusions
rows.statement: Lists ten candidate recurring architectural distinctions to be tested against the actual Steps-1-182 evidence rather than accepted by default (Identity!=State, Knowledge!=Authority, Decision!=Execution, Execution!=Outcome, Unknown!=False, CurrentState!=History, Generation!=Validation, Validation!=Authorization, Claim->Evidence, Context_A!=Context_B), explicitly labelled candidates pending evidence.

rows.anchor: They are all forms of: A ≠ B where software engineering frequently makes the mistake: A ≈ B ... restoring distinctions that had been collapsed
rows.statement: Identifies a deeper common structure across the recurring principles: each is an instance of A!=B guarding against a common engineering mistake of collapsing A~=B (Identity~=State, Prediction~=Truth, Knowledge~=Authority, Execution~=Outcome), proposing this pattern-of-restoring-collapsed-distinctions as possibly one of the deepest architectural themes in the entire book.

rows.anchor: Robust knowledge-centric software depends on preserving distinctions that carry semantic, temporal, epistemic or governance meaning ... SemanticIntegrity ∝ DistinctionPreservation ... a hypothesis, not a proven theorem
rows.statement: States the 'distinction preservation' hypothesis (robust knowledge-centric software depends on preserving semantically/temporally/epistemically/governance-meaningful distinctions), formalized as SemanticIntegrity proportional-to DistinctionPreservation, explicitly labelled a hypothesis to be tested against the Steps-1-182 evidence rather than a proven theorem; connects this across DDD (Entity!=ValueObject), mathematics (x!=y), statistics (Observed!=Inferred, Correlation!=Causation), governance (Capability!=Authority) and AI engineering (Generation!=Verification) as convergent instances of one meta-principle: do not collapse distinctions that matter.

rows.anchor: Krishna ~ Perspective possessing continuity across changing manifestations ... What would a software system need if it were required to preserve continuity across changing states? ... Versioning, Provenance, History, Lineage, Context
rows.statement: Proposes a careful literary (not architectural) interpretation of Krishna as 'a perspective possessing continuity across changing manifestations', translating this into the engineering question of what a system needs to preserve continuity across changing states (versioning, provenance, history, lineage, context), explicitly warning against the trivializing claim 'Krishna is the system's memory'.

rows.anchor: Philosophical Analogy ≠ Technical Proof ... Outcome A ... retrospective analogy ... Outcome B ... repeatedly influenced ... Outcome C ... independently emerged technically and philosophically ... the most interesting result
rows.statement: States three possible historical outcomes for the Gita lens's actual role to be determined by the reconstruction rather than assumed: (A) it was purely a retrospective analogy applied after the fact, (B) it repeatedly and genuinely influenced engineering questions during development, (C) the same principles independently emerged both technically and philosophically -- rated the most interesting possible result, expressible as EngineeringObservation<->PhilosophicalReflection without either proving the other.

rows.anchor: Suppose a technical invariant existed before the corresponding Gītā reflection ... TechnicalDiscovery -> PhilosophicalRecognition ... those are different histories. The Evidence Ledger will tell us which actually occurred
rows.statement: States that chronology determines which of two different intellectual histories occurred (technical discovery preceding philosophical recognition, or vice versa) and that only the actual Evidence Ledger -- not narrative preference -- can establish which; reframes Step 215's most important task as determining 'when did the idea enter the reasoning', not merely what was concluded.

rows.anchor: 182 Steps -> 43 SignificantEvents -> 17 CoreInsights -> 8 ArchitecturalPrinciples -> 4 MajorThemes. The exact numbers are unknown
rows.statement: Proposes a compression pipeline reducing 182 raw steps to a small number of significant events, core insights, architectural principles, and major themes (illustrative counts only, explicitly not fixed), arguing the book should present the intellectual structure hidden inside the steps rather than the 182 steps themselves; proposes an intermediate 5-epoch structure (Problem Recognition -> Experimentation -> DDD/Domain Modeling -> Mathematical/Epistemic Formalization -> KnowledgeOS/AI-Engineering Architecture) explicitly not to be frozen before the evidence determines it.

rows.anchor: Architecture_observed ... Architecture_designed ... Architecture_implemented ... Architecture_proposed ... Observed ≠ Intended ≠ Implemented ≠ Target
rows.statement: Warns that the single word 'architecture' conflates at least four distinct referents (observed, intended, implemented, target/proposed) that may differ from each other, proposing Observed!=Intended!=Implemented!=Target as a central reconstruction rule; separately notes that linguistic markers in generated text ('should' signals P, 'the code contains' signals F if verified, 'therefore requires' signals D) can help automatically classify epistemic status at scale.

rows.anchor: Step Source Artifact Date/Sequence Primary Topic Type Observation Fact Hypothesis Experiment Result Derived Insight Decision Rejected Alternative Architectural Principle Invariant Evidence Gita Connection Status [F/D/P/U] Confidence Open Question
rows.statement: Specifies the Step 215 Artifact: a 19-column Master Reconstruction Matrix schema intended as the master source for eventual book-writing, including a dedicated 'Gita Connection' column and 'Rejected Alternative' column.

lineage_claims.quote: The next concrete deliverable should therefore be: Step 215 Artifact — Master Reconstruction Matrix

rows.anchor: Do not: rewrite the book; freeze the chapter structure; invent missing evidence; merge competing concepts; eliminate contradictions; assume implementation ... Reconstruct. Analyze. Synthesize. Write.
rows.statement: Lists nine things not to do before reconstruction is complete (rewrite the book, freeze chapter structure, invent missing evidence, merge competing concepts, eliminate contradictions, assume implementation, over-architect philosophical analogies, assign arbitrary percentages, create formulas for their own sake), sequencing the correct order as Reconstruct -> Analyze -> Synthesize -> Write.

rows.anchor: Phase 1 — Archaeology ... Phase 2 — Separation of Concerns ... Phase 3 — Synthesis ... This is the correct point at which Claude should eventually begin chapter-by-chapter writing. Not before
rows.statement: Defines a three-phase book-production architecture: Phase 1 Archaeology (S1..S182 -> Evidence Ledger, understand what happened), Phase 2 Separation of Concerns (separate Facts from Derivations from Proposals from PhilosophicalInterpretations, preventing conceptual contamination), Phase 3 Synthesis (Evidence->Patterns->Principles->Architecture->Book), stating chapter-by-chapter writing is correct only after all three phases, not before.

rows.anchor: B = Synthesize(Evidence,Experiments,Failures,Insights,Architecture,PhilosophicalReflection) ... ClaimStrength ≤ EvidenceStrength ... PhilosophicalReflection ≠ TechnicalEvidence ... CurrentArchitecture ≠ TargetArchitecture
rows.statement: States the final synthesis equation for the whole book-generation process, B=Synthesize(Evidence,Experiments,Failures,Insights,Architecture,PhilosophicalReflection), subject to three boxed constraints (ClaimStrength<=EvidenceStrength, PhilosophicalReflection!=TechnicalEvidence, CurrentArchitecture!=TargetArchitecture), explicitly framed as protecting the book against retrospective rewriting, overclaiming, and confusing philosophy with engineering proof.

rows.anchor: It should be the actual execution of the reconstruction ... I should not fabricate their contents from the current conversation ... Once they are available here, we can process them in batches
rows.statement: Previews Step 216: not another theoretical step but the actual execution of the reconstruction, explicitly refusing to fabricate the contents of Steps 1-182 from memory/conversation and requiring the real historical artifacts to be brought in and processed in batches, after which Step 183 onward may need renaming or absorption into the synthesis.

lineage_claims.quote: I recommend that Step 216 should not be another theoretical step.

rows.anchor: each file's tail contains the agenda for the next step
rows.statement: Structural observation, load-bearing for the whole verification: each file in the 208-215 band ends with the agenda section for the *next* step (e.g. the file titled 'Step 208' ends with a '# Step 209' section at line 1423 onward), so the band is a chain of overlapping documents and every 'Step N' agenda exists in two places (as the prior file's tail and the next file's own opening).

rows.anchor: IT SPECIFIES A METHOD. It reconstructs nothing.
rows.statement: Exhaustive machine count of every step-index token in Step 215 ('Reconstruct Steps 1-182'): of the 182 steps, only 6 are individually named (1, 2, 3, 73, 91, 182), 0 are quoted, 0 are given any content, 0 are given a substantive verdict, and 176 never appear at all. The file's only data matrix (Section 215.5) has 40 cells (8 columns x 5 rows): 28 are the placeholder '...' and 12 are filled, all with step index/type-tag/status-tag -- zero cells contain information about any of the 182 steps. Step 215 itself concedes 'the exact contents must come from the actual saved artifacts, not memory or invention,' and names its own future deliverable, the 'Step 215 Artifact — Master Reconstruction Matrix,' as not yet produced.

rows.anchor: the two live step indices used as notation examples do not match the real corpus steps they name
rows.statement: Verifiable error in Step 215's notation examples: Step 91's real corpus file is titled 'Formal Specification and Refinement', but Step 215 tags it 'EXP + F' (an experimentally established fact); under Step 215's own taxonomy (Section 215.3) a formal-specification step should be tagged MAT or VER, not EXP. Step 73 ('Identity, Trust and Cryptographic Provenance') tagged 'ARC + D' is defensible and not called an error. The Step 91 mismatch's status is ambiguous as to intent (possibly pure notation demonstration) but unambiguous as to fact: the tag does not describe the step it names. Not silently repaired.

rows.anchor: 'Evidence' is a CATEGORY NAME. It is a node label in an arrow diagram.
rows.statement: Step 215's boxed objective S_1...S_182 -> Evidence -> Knowledge -> Architecture uses 'Evidence' as an unpopulated category/column name, not as actual evidence: no evidence item is exhibited anywhere in the file, 'Evidence' appears only as an unpopulated column header (all '...') in the reconstruction matrix and the Master Reconstruction Matrix column list, and Section 215.31 restates the same arrow as a *future* Phase 1 workflow step ('Understand what actually happened', future tense). The arrow is therefore DEFINED on the computability ladder and no further -- its inputs (the 182 artifacts) are NOT KNOWN to the file, and Step 216's own preview concedes the historical artifacts are not yet available.

rows.anchor: THE CUT-OFF IS NOWHERE JUSTIFIED. It is asserted six times and defended zero times.
rows.statement: The Steps-1-182 cutoff in Step 215 is asserted at six locations (title, line 26, line 343, line 770, line 1024, line 1156) but never justified anywhere in the file or in Steps 212-214. What happens to Steps 183-214 is explicitly deferred to an undated future decision ('we can return to the sequential architecture work and decide whether what we previously called Step 183 onward still makes sense'), leaving a 29-33 step remainder unreconciled against Step 212's own claim that derivation ran through Step 211.

rows.anchor: the corpus contradicts itself on the scope of the derivation phase
rows.statement: Step 212 Section 212.5 states 'Steps 1-211 have largely been derivation,' while Step 212 Section 212.33 scopes the reconstruction to 'the artifacts already generated during Steps 1-182 and later implementation material' -- so the corpus declares derivation runs 1-211 while reconstruction covers only 1-182, and the resulting 29-33-step gap is never reconciled anywhere in the band.

rows.anchor: SELF-EXEMPTION (the most consequential finding about Step 215's scope)
rows.statement: Steps 183-215 (which include all eight in-scope files of this verification) are placed outside the evidence discipline Step 215 itself mandates for Steps 1-182. Concretely, Step 213 Section 213.26 mandates that every important statement during reconstruction should carry an [F]/[D]/[P]/[U] label, but a machine count of applied labels in Steps 213, 214 and 215 finds 4, 0, 0 respectively -- and all four occurrences in 213 are the four lines of the legend itself. Applied labels across the three files that mandate them: zero. Not one claim in 208-215 carries the epistemic label those same files declare mandatory.

rows.anchor: The band is a five-deep chain of deferral
rows.statement: Step 215 produces a 14-code type taxonomy (glossary), a 20-column header list (text fence), a 5-row placeholder matrix (28/40 cells '...'), a 3-phase workflow, and a closing pointer to Step 216 -- i.e. FORWARD POINTER, not an artifact. Verbatim deferral chain: 212->213 ('the next stage should be an evidence-driven reconstruction'); 213->214 ('create the first Evidence Ledger'); 214->215 ('the next step should be retrospective reconstruction'); 215->216 ('Step 216 should not be another theoretical step... it should be the actual execution of the reconstruction'); 216->? ('we should not yet write another architectural theory step', out of scope). Four consecutive files each announce that the *next* file will do the empirical work; the audit announced in Step 212 has not begun by the end of Step 215.

rows.anchor: Recurring principles we already appear to have discovered
rows.statement: Step 215 Section 215.8 asserts (in the indicative, warranted only by 'from the progression of our work') that ten recurring principles (Identity!=State, Knowledge!=Authority, Decision!=Execution, Execution!=Outcome, Unknown!=False, CurrentState!=History, Generation!=Validation, Validation!=Authorization, Claim->Evidence, Context_A!=Context_B) have appeared repeatedly, calling them 'candidate principles, not yet declared final conclusions.' The hedge covers only finality, not the antecedent claim that they recur -- recurrence across 182 steps is asserted with zero instances cited. Section 215.7 names the exact quantity that would substantiate this, Convergence(I) = NumberOfIndependentEvidencePaths(I), explicitly declines to turn it into a numerical score, and computes it for exactly zero of the ten principles: DEFINED but not INPUTS_KNOWN, not CONSTRUCTIBLE, not COMPUTED.

rows.anchor: Our architecture repeatedly responds by restoring distinctions that had been collapsed
rows.statement: Step 215 Section 215.9 claims 'our architecture repeatedly responds by restoring distinctions that had been collapsed' and calls this 'one of the deepest architectural themes in the entire book.' 'Repeatedly responds' is an unhedged claim about the historical record of Steps 1-182; not one such response is located in any step, only the second sentence ('may be one of the deepest') is properly hedged.

rows.anchor: The 'distinction preservation' hypothesis — MEASUREMENT VERDICT: ILL-TYPED
rows.statement: Step 215 Section 215.10 boxes the hypothesis 'Robust knowledge-centric software depends on preserving distinctions that carry semantic, temporal, epistemic or governance meaning,' formalized as SemanticIntegrity proportional to DistinctionPreservation, and calls it 'a hypothesis, not a proven theorem' to be tested by the Steps 1-182 reconstruction. Judged the worst-formed formal object in the band: proportionality (∝) requires both sides to lie on a ratio scale (non-arbitrary zero, meaningful ratios); SemanticIntegrity has no unit/zero/ordering/operational definition anywhere in the band (the nearest prior object is Step 208's Boolean SI(C,B)=True, which admits no proportionality), and DistinctionPreservation is never defined at all in 208-215. Consequently the statement is not false but not truth-apt -- no observation could confirm or refute it, so the reconstruction Step 215 assigns to test it cannot test it as written. This is the FIRST INVALID INFERENCE in Step 215; everything downstream that depends on it (including Section 215.12's candidate book thesis, a natural-language restatement of the same unmeasurable proportionality) is conditional on repairing it.

rows.anchor: Step 215 Section 215.30's nine-item self-restraint clause
rows.statement: Step 215 Section 215.30 lists nine prohibitions for the reconstruction ('do not: rewrite the book; freeze the chapter structure; invent missing evidence; merge competing concepts; eliminate contradictions; assume implementation; turn every philosophical analogy into architecture; assign arbitrary percentages; create more theoretical formulas merely because we can'), credited as the corpus's best self-discipline clause to date. Step 215 complies with 7 of the 9 prohibitions but violates 'create more theoretical formulas merely because we can' by minting Convergence(I), R(S_i), and the boxed proportionality all in the same file, and stands in weak tension with 'invent missing evidence' by asserting recurrence (Section 215.8-215.9) without exhibiting it.

rows.anchor: Further arithmetic checks: 0.87>=0.80 correct; 0.91+/-0.08 within range at 1 sigma but 2-sigma bound exceeds 1; ratio checks disclaimed
rows.statement: Additional independently-verified arithmetic in the band: Step 209 Section 209.15's 0.87 >= 0.80 evaluates to True (correct). Step 208 Section 208.14 / Step 210 Section 210.12's 0.91 +/- 0.08 gives [0.83, 0.99], within [0,1] at 1-sigma, but at 2-sigma the upper bound is 1.07 > 1 -- out of range for a quantity called 'confidence', though the corpus never commits this specific error since the interval's coverage level is left unlabelled. Step 215 Section 215.24's ratios (182/43=4.233, 43/17=2.529, 17/8=2.125, 8/4=2.0, total 45.5x) make no arithmetic claim and are correctly disclaimed as unknown. Step 209 Section 209.42 vs Step 210 Section 210.25: |I_KOS|=8 vs |{I1..I15}|=15, difference 7, mapping absent (unreconciled).

rows.anchor: PREVIOUS DEPENDENCY (cited BY NUMBER). ZERO individual steps — only two ranges (Steps 1-211, Steps 1-182)
rows.statement: Step 212 cites no individual prior step by number, only two ranges (Steps 1-211 in Section 212.5, Steps 1-182 in Section 212.33). Later response in scope: Step 213 adopts the epistemic discipline and recasts it as F/D/P/U; Step 215 Section 215.30's prohibition on 'assume implementation' echoes Step 212 Section 212.32.

rows.anchor: PREVIOUS DEPENDENCY: ZERO individual prior steps (one range, Steps 1-182); LATER RESPONSE: Steps 214 and 215 both build on F/D/P/U
rows.statement: Step 213 cites zero individual prior steps by number, only the Steps-1-182 range (in the Step-214 preview). Later response in scope: Step 214 Section 214.1 operationalizes F/D/P/U into the 10-tuple EL_i; Step 215 Section 215.4 adopts F/D/P/U as its second classification axis.

rows.anchor: FORMAL OBJECTS: R(S_i)=(O_i,L_i,A_i,V_i,U_i); StepCount != KnowledgeCount; the 3-phase book pipeline B=Synthesize(...)
rows.statement: Step 215 ('Reconstruct Steps 1-182') proposes, for every step S_i, a 5-slot record R(S_i)=(O_i,L_i,A_i,V_i,U_i); boxes StepCount != KnowledgeCount; boxes 'Type x EpistemicStatus' (the 14-code type taxonomy crossed with F/D/P/U); poses 'which architectural principles appear independently more than once?' and defines Convergence(I)=NumberOfIndependentEvidencePaths(I); boxes the distinction-preservation hypothesis SemanticIntegrity ∝ DistinctionPreservation and 'do not collapse distinctions that matter'; boxes 'Philosophical Analogy != Technical Proof'; states 182 Steps -> 43 SignificantEvents -> 17 CoreInsights -> 8 ArchitecturalPrinciples -> 4 MajorThemes and Epoch_1->...->Epoch_5; boxes Observed != Intended != Implemented != Target; boxes the synthesis functional B=Synthesize(Evidence,Experiments,Failures,Insights,Architecture,PhilosophicalReflection); and boxes ClaimStrength <= EvidenceStrength and PhilosophicalReflection != TechnicalEvidence.

rows.anchor: ARITY MISMATCH (Section 215.1): six questions asked, five slots given — the missing slot is question 1, 'What happened?'
rows.statement: Section 215.1 asks six questions per step (what happened, what was observed, what was learned, what architectural consequence followed, what was actually verified, what remained unknown) but produces R(S_i)=(O_i,L_i,A_i,V_i,U_i), only five slots, mapping O=observed(Q2), L=learned(Q3), A=architectural(Q4), V=verified(Q5), U=unknown(Q6) -- Question 1, 'what happened?', has no field, in a step whose entire purpose is reconstructing what happened.

rows.anchor: Secondary invalid inference: the 'A != B' generalization is drawn from surface notation, and one of its ten instances does not have that form
rows.statement: Section 215.9 infers a shared substance from a shared syntactic form ('they are all forms of A!=B where software engineering frequently makes the mistake A~=B'), but the ten cited propositions share only notation, not mechanism: Identity!=State is ontological, Unknown!=False is a three-valued-logic requirement, Execution!=Outcome is causal/observational, and Claim->Evidence (item 9) is an implication, not of the form A!=B at all, though the file lists it among 'all forms of A!=B' regardless.

rows.anchor: COMPUTABILITY: Master Reconstruction Matrix DEFINED (20 column names) with 0 rows; Synthesize never specified; epochs explicitly not frozen
rows.statement: R(S_i) is DEFINED (5-ary, for 6 questions) but computed for 0 of 182 steps; the 14-code taxonomy is DEFINED and applied to 6 step indices as notation demos, 0 substantively; Convergence(I) is DEFINED but computed for 0 of 10 principles; the Master Reconstruction Matrix is DEFINED (20 column names) with 0 rows; B=Synthesize(...) is DEFINED but Synthesize is never specified; Epochs are DEFINED but explicitly not frozen ('we should not freeze these as the actual epochs yet'). TEST VERDICT NOT_EXECUTED.

rows.anchor: STATISTICAL VERDICT: MIXED — the Gita-role hypothesis space with a chronological discriminator is the best-designed unexecuted test in the corpus
rows.statement: Convergence(I) as a count of independent evidence paths is statistically the right notion (independence is what makes replication informative), and Section 215.7 correctly declines to convert it into a quality score. Section 215.21's three-outcome hypothesis space for the Gita chapters' actual role (A: retrospective analogy; B: genuine influence; C: independent convergence) with Section 215.22's chronological discriminating test ('suppose a technical invariant existed before the corresponding Gita reflection') is judged the best-designed unexecuted test in the corpus -- falsifiable, with an observable discriminating variable (timestamps) correctly identified. Incorrect: the proportionality in Section 215.10; unsupported: the recurrence claim of Section 215.8.

rows.anchor: DDD VERDICT: MIXED — the recurring-!= observation across disciplines is worthwhile; the four architecture senses are the file's most durable contribution
rows.statement: Section 215.11's observation that DDD, mathematics, statistics, governance and AI engineering all trade in != relations (Entity!=ValueObject, Aggregate!=DatabaseTable, Context_A!=Context_B, Correlation!=Causation, Capability!=Authority, Generation!=Verification) is a real and worthwhile cross-discipline observation. Sections 215.26-215.27's four architecture senses (Observed!=Intended!=Implemented!=Target) is judged a genuinely useful DDD-governance distinction and the file's most durable contribution. Deficiency: Aggregate!=DatabaseTable and Context_A!=Context_B are asserted with no actual Step 205 aggregate or Step 206 context pair examined -- the DDD content is entirely illustrative.

rows.anchor: UL NOTES: the Krishna metaphor handled with genuine restraint; six overlapping classification vocabularies over the same ground, never cross-mapped
rows.statement: Section 215.19 handles the Krishna metaphor with genuine care, refusing 'Krishna is the system's memory' as trivializing, and reframing it as 'Krishna ~ Perspective possessing continuity across changing manifestations'; Section 215.20 boxes Philosophical Analogy != Technical Proof. This lens/proof boundary is maintained consistently across the whole band (208.33, 209.40, 210.37, 212.27, 213.15, 214.25, 215.13-21) -- no overreach found, a genuine strength. Against this, the 14 type codes overlap the corpus's other classification vocabularies (Step 212's 5 statuses, Step 213's 4 F/D/P/U labels, Step 214's 8 KStates, Step 211's C0-C4 and 6 assurance dimensions) with no cross-mapping anywhere -- six classification vocabularies over overlapping ground in eight files.

rows.anchor: ASSUMPTIONS / HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS — the 182 boundary is never argued and Convergence may be identically 1 in a single-author sequential corpus
rows.statement: Stated: Steps 1-182 are the meaningful unit; independent recurrence indicates depth; chronology is recoverable from the artifacts. Hidden: that 182 is the right boundary (never argued, and contradicted by Step 212 Section 212.5's 'Steps 1-211'); that the reconstructor can access the 182 artifacts (the Step 216 preview says they are not yet available); that independent evidence paths are identifiable -- Convergence(I) needs an independence criterion, none is given, and in a single-author sequential corpus no two steps are plausibly independent, which may make Convergence identically 1; that distinction-preservation is measurable (required by Section 215.10, false as the band stands). Undefined symbols: SemanticIntegrity, DistinctionPreservation, Synthesize(.), NumberOfIndependentEvidencePaths(.) and 'independent', P_1/P_7/P_31 (Section 215.6, never defined, ambiguous whether steps or principles), O_i/L_i/A_i/V_i/U_i (declared by position only), every Epoch_n.

rows.anchor: WHAT SURVIVES / WHAT DOES NOT SURVIVE — Step 215
rows.statement: Survives: StepCount != KnowledgeCount; the 14-code taxonomy as a working instrument; Observed != Intended != Implemented != Target; Philosophical Analogy != Technical Proof and the Krishna restraint; the three-outcome Gita hypothesis with the chronological discriminator (the best-designed unexecuted test in the corpus); Section 215.30's nine-item prohibition list; ClaimStrength <= EvidenceStrength; the three-phase pipeline as a plan. Does not survive: the title; SemanticIntegrity ∝ DistinctionPreservation; R(S_i) as specified (5 slots for 6 questions); the recurrence claim (215.8) and the 'repeatedly responds' claim (215.9), both unevidenced; the A!=B generalization (one of ten instances is not of that form); any reconstruction of any step.

rows.anchor: Tuple arity drift: 'the ledger' alone is specified at five different arities across two files

aliases: Multi-Agent Knowledge, Conflict Resolution, Consensus, Trust and Distributed Epistemics

sources.note: S0913's Step 25U: the fully worked multi-agent trust/conflict/consensus model (contextual trust, competence tables, evidence-clustered consensus, ByzantineConsensus distinction); extends B0021's authority-trust-source-reliability-knowledge-commitment (S0876/Step 19) with a formal conflict taxonomy and resolution pipeline.

rows.anchor: \mathcal A=\{Human,LLM,System,Sensor,Database,Agent,ExternalAuthority\} ... What should KnowledgeOS do when credible sources disagree? ... not pick the source with the highest confidence
rows.statement: Extends the model to a seven-type set of independent epistemic producers, framing the central question of what to do when credible sources disagree, explicitly rejecting 'pick the source with the highest confidence.'

rows.anchor: Agent\neq Evidence ... The scanner itself is not the observation. The observation is E ... ProducedBy(E)=Agent
rows.statement: States Agent ≠ Evidence: an agent produces evidence, provenance recorded as ProducedBy(E)=Agent, worked with an InfrastructureScanner example.

rows.anchor: AgentID and AgentType\in\{Human,AI,System,Sensor,Organization,Authority\} ... without treating them as equivalent sources
rows.statement: Requires every epistemic actor to have stable AgentID and AgentType (six-value enum), preventing treatment of dissimilar sources as equivalent.

rows.anchor: Trust(Agent)=0.9 ... too simplistic ... Trust(a,d,c,t) ... Trust(AI,CodeAnalysis,RepositoryX) may be high ... Trust(AI,LegalApproval) may be irrelevant
rows.statement: Rejects a bare scalar Trust(Agent)=0.9, requiring contextual Trust(a,d,c,t) parameterized by domain/context/time, worked with a code-analysis-vs-legal-approval contrast.

rows.anchor: Expertise=High but AuthorityToApproveArchitecture=False ... Expertise\neq Authority ... Trust\neq Authority
rows.statement: Distinguishes Expertise from Authority (a highly expert engineer may lack architecture-approval authority; an authoritative Board may not be the best source for a low-level measurement) — Expertise ≠ Authority, Trust ≠ Authority.

rows.anchor: Reliability(Source) from Trust(Agent) ... an architect's recollection of an IP address ... highly trustworthy [but] low reliability for exact network facts
rows.statement: Distinguishes Reliability(Source) from Trust(Agent): a generally trustworthy source can still be unreliable for a specific measurement type.

rows.anchor: Agent A and B both read Vendor Document ... AgentIndependence\neq InformationIndependence ... extends the double-counting principle from 25N
rows.statement: States AgentIndependence ≠ InformationIndependence: two distinct agents reading the same document are not thereby independent sources — explicitly extends the double-counting principle from Step 25N.

rows.anchor: Counting A and B as two independent confirmations would inflate confidence. The actual independent information may be approximately 1 source
rows.statement: Worked common-source-dependency example: two agents both reading one vendor document should count as approximately one independent information unit, not two.

rows.anchor: G_D=(V,E_D) ... E_1\leftarrow SourceDocument, E_2\leftarrow SourceDocument ... E_1\not\perp E_2
rows.statement: Defines a dependency graph G_D=(V,E_D) for evidence provenance, enabling detection of non-independence (E1 ⊥̸ E2) among evidence sharing a common source.

rows.anchor: Conflict(A,E_1,E_2) ... same entity? same time? same context? same proposition? same measurement? independently acquired? authoritative? different scopes? Only then can we resolve the conflict
rows.statement: Defines Conflict(A,E1,E2) and requires an eight-question diagnostic checklist (entity, time, context, proposition, measurement, independent acquisition, authority, differing scopes) before attempting resolution.

rows.anchor: Nexus=3.69 at 10:00, Nexus=3.70 at 15:00 ... Conflict=False ... identity + temporal semantics must precede conflict resolution
rows.statement: Worked apparent-conflict example resolved by temporal disambiguation (different times) — Conflict=False; identity+temporal semantics must precede conflict resolution.

rows.anchor: Nexus_{production}=3.70 and Nexus_{development}=3.69 ... Conflict=False. The apparent contradiction disappears after entity/context resolution
rows.statement: Worked apparent-conflict example resolved by context/entity disambiguation (production vs development) — again Conflict=False.

rows.anchor: ProductionNexus=3.69 at t=10:00 and ProductionNexus=3.70 at the same t=10:00 ... genuine conflict. KnowledgeOS must preserve it
rows.statement: Worked genuine-conflict example: same entity, same time, contradictory values — must be preserved, not disambiguated away.

rows.anchor: if conflict: choose one, delete the other. That destroys epistemic history ... Conflict=FirstClassKnowledgeState
rows.statement: Warns against the anti-pattern of silently choosing and deleting one side of a conflict, destroying epistemic history — Conflict must be a FirstClassKnowledgeState.

rows.anchor: ResolveConflict(E_1,E_2,A,C)\rightarrow Resolution ... Confirmed(E_1), Confirmed(E_2), BothValid, BothInvalid, Unresolved
rows.statement: Defines ResolveConflict(E1,E2,A,C)->Resolution with five possible outcomes: Confirmed(E1), Confirmed(E2), BothValid, BothInvalid, Unresolved.

rows.anchor: Temperature_1=20C and Temperature_2=21C ... may both be correct because they measure different physical locations ... Conflict may actually indicate ContextMissing
rows.statement: Worked BothValid example: two sensors at different physical locations both correct — a reported Conflict may actually indicate ContextMissing, 'a very important diagnostic principle.'

rows.anchor: Conflict->Identity check->Temporal check->Context check->Semantic proposition check->Dependency check->Source reliability->Authority->Independent corroboration->Resolution/Unresolved ... much safer than weighted voting
rows.statement: Presents a nine-stage conflict-resolution pipeline, explicitly 'much safer than weighted voting.'

rows.anchor: Trust(A)=0.8 and Trust(B)=0.7 ... should not calculate 0.8>0.7\Rightarrow A=True ... B may possess direct contradictory evidence. A may merely be repeating B's source ... TrustScore\neq TruthSelector
rows.statement: Warns against naive trust-score comparison to resolve conflicts: a higher-trust source may merely repeat a lower-trust source's own contradictory direct evidence — TrustScore ≠ TruthSelector.

rows.anchor: Architecture Board approved migration [engineer] versus Architecture Board rejected migration [official record] ... official decision record has stronger authority ... B can supersede A for governance status. But A should remain historical evidence
rows.statement: Worked authority-resolved conflict example: an official decision record supersedes an ordinary engineer's claim for governance status, while the engineer's claim remains historical evidence.

rows.anchor: System: Nexus version=3.69 versus LLM: Nexus version appears to be 3.70 ... not because System>LLM universally. It is because MeasurementMethod is better suited to that proposition
rows.statement: Argues preferring a direct system observation over an LLM interpretation is a measurement-method-suitability judgment for that specific proposition, not a universal source-type ranking.

rows.anchor: Competence(a,q) ... much more meaningful than a global trust score
rows.statement: Defines Competence(a,q) (agent competence per question type), worked with a six-row table (production API/network scanner/architect/Architecture Board/LLM-synthesis high, LLM-authoritative-approval not sufficient) — 'much more meaningful than a global trust score.'

rows.anchor: Calibration(a) or Accuracy(a) ... ErrorRate(a) ... Reliability(a,q,t) ... reputation should itself be evidence-based and versioned
rows.statement: Defines reputation via historical Calibration/Accuracy/ErrorRate feeding Reliability(a,q,t), requiring reputation itself to be evidence-based and versioned.

rows.anchor: A produces evidence supporting its own previous conclusions ... increase A's apparent reliability ... FeedbackBias ... trust must not be allowed to recursively reinforce itself without independent validation
rows.statement: Warns of self-reinforcing FeedbackBias: an agent's own evidence inflating its own apparent reliability without independent validation.

rows.anchor: ReliabilityAssessment: Agent=Scanner-01 ... Basis: 4892 validated observations ... FalsePositiveRate: 0.2% ... Now trust is itself an epistemic object
rows.statement: Worked structured trust/reliability-provenance record, making trust itself an evidence-carrying epistemic object.

rows.anchor: TrustAssessment as a derived knowledge object ... evidence; evaluation period; domain; method; uncertainty; revision history ... prevents trust from becoming magic metadata
rows.statement: Defines TrustAssessment as a derived knowledge object with six required fields, preventing trust from becoming 'magic metadata.'

rows.anchor: MajorityAgreement, WeightedAgreement, IndependentEvidenceConvergence ... not equivalent ... I prefer IndependentEvidenceConvergence over simple agent voting
rows.statement: Distinguishes three non-equivalent consensus definitions, preferring IndependentEvidenceConvergence over simple agent voting.

rows.anchor: Agent A,B,C -> Source X ... three agents agree but there is one underlying source ... System API, Filesystem, Human -> E1,E2,E3 ... the second provides substantially stronger corroboration
rows.statement: Contrasts three agents citing one source (weak corroboration) with three genuinely independent acquisition paths (strong corroboration).

rows.anchor: C_1,\ldots,C_n independent evidence clusters ... consensus is evaluated across C_i rather than raw agents ... prevents source duplication from artificially increasing support
rows.statement: States consensus should be evaluated over independent evidence clusters, not raw agent counts, preventing source-duplication inflation.

rows.anchor: k independent confirmations ... k=2 ... especially useful for high-impact operations. But again k=2 is a domain policy, not a universal epistemic law
rows.statement: Defines a quorum requirement (k independent confirmations) as domain policy, not a universal epistemic law.

rows.anchor: EpistemicConflict\neq ByzantineConsensus ... Byzantine consensus asks can nodes agree despite faulty nodes; KnowledgeOS asks which proposition is epistemically justified given evidence of different quality and provenance ... EvidenceQuality must remain distinct from NodeCount
rows.statement: Explicitly distinguishes EpistemicConflict from Byzantine consensus: the problems overlap but are not identical since KnowledgeOS asks which proposition is epistemically justified, not merely whether nodes can agree — 'a truthful minority with direct evidence may be more valuable than a majority repeating weak evidence' — EvidenceQuality ≠ NodeCount.

rows.anchor: Architect A: migration is safe / Architect B: migration is unsafe ... should not immediately calculate 50%/50% ... often disagreement is actually ModelDifference rather than FactDifference
rows.statement: Worked human-disagreement example: two architects' conflicting risk assessments should not be treated as a 50/50 split without checking whether the disagreement is really ModelDifference rather than FactDifference.

rows.anchor: M_1 predicts Risk=5% while M_2 predicts Risk=20% ... both may use the same evidence ... Conflict is not in the observations. It is in Models
rows.statement: Worked model-disagreement example: two models producing different risk numbers from identical evidence shows the conflict lives in the models, not the observations — 'a critical distinction.'

rows.anchor: ConflictType=\{IdentityConflict,TemporalConflict,ContextConflict,MeasurementConflict,SemanticConflict,EvidenceConflict,ModelConflict,PolicyConflict,AuthorityConflict\}
rows.statement: Defines a nine-value ConflictType taxonomy, 'much more useful than one generic conflict=true.'

rows.anchor: Resolution=(Conflict,Method,Evidence,Decision,Authority,ResidualUncertainty) ... excellent auditability
rows.statement: Defines a six-field Resolution object, worked with a Nexus-version-conflict example resolved via direct production API observation, retaining a ResidualUncertainty note (API cache freshness) — 'excellent auditability.'

rows.anchor: Resolution=Unresolved ... does not mean the system failed ... AvailableEvidence does not justify selecting one proposition ... Zero can represent UnresolvedConflict
rows.statement: States Unresolved is a valid terminal state, not a system failure, feeding Zero=UnresolvedConflict.

rows.anchor: Lord may determine NextAction=AcquireIndependentEvidence ... query production package manager ... Conflict->Zero->Lord->Evidence->Resolution
rows.statement: Worked example of Lord resolving an unresolved conflict via a targeted independent-evidence-acquisition action, closing the Conflict->Zero->Lord->Evidence->Resolution loop.

rows.anchor: Agent A,B,C,D -> Evidence -> Assessment -> Knowledge -> Conflict? {No->Accept, Yes->Zero->Lord->New information} ... a very strong architecture
rows.statement: Presents the full multi-agent epistemic loop diagram integrating multiple agents' evidence through assessment, knowledge, a conflict branch, and the Zero/Lord follow-up path.

rows.anchor: I would avoid a generic AgentManager ... EpistemicActor and domain-specific TrustPolicy, ConflictPolicy, AuthorityPolicy ... the domain decides what counts as sufficient agreement
rows.statement: Rejects a generic AgentManager owning all semantics, proposing a bounded-context-neutral EpistemicActor infrastructure plus domain-specific TrustPolicy/ConflictPolicy/AuthorityPolicy.

rows.anchor: Actor=(ActorID,Type,Capabilities,AuthorityScopes,Provenance) ... capabilities ... should not be assumed from actor type. They are explicit
rows.statement: Defines a five-field Actor object with explicit (not type-inferred) Capabilities such as observe/interpret/derive/approve/execute.

rows.anchor: CanExecuteDeployment=True but AuthorizedToExecute=False ... CanRecommend=True but CanApprove=False ... preserves our previous separation
rows.statement: Restates capability-vs-authority separation for actors: technical capability to execute/recommend does not imply authorization/approval standing.

rows.anchor: CanObserve(X), CanAssert(X), CanDerive(X), CanApprove(X), CanExecute(X) ... different privileges ... highly relevant to enterprise governance
rows.statement: Defines five distinct epistemic permissions (CanObserve, CanAssert, CanDerive, CanApprove, CanExecute) as different privileges, relevant to enterprise governance.

rows.anchor: Trust(A)=1.0 does not give Authority(A,ApproveChange) ... Trust never substitutes for authority
rows.statement: States the architectural invariant: even maximal trust does not confer authority — 'Trust never substitutes for authority.'

rows.anchor: Trust(A)=High does not mean A's assertion=True ... Trust modifies epistemic weight; it does not create truth
rows.statement: States trust modifies the assessment of evidence but does not create evidence or truth — 'Trust modifies epistemic weight; it does not create truth.'

rows.anchor: P(H)=\sum_i Trust_i ... we cannot simply use this ... must account for source dependence; reliability; false positives; false negatives; prior beliefs; measurement uncertainty
rows.statement: Rejects naive summed-trust probability aggregation P(H)=sum Trust_i, requiring the evidence model to account for source dependence, reliability, false-positive/negative rates, priors, and measurement uncertainty.

rows.anchor: LR_1=19, LR_2=15 ... if independent LR_{combined}=285 ... but if both are derived from the same document, LR_{combined} must not automatically be 285 ... directly connects 25U to 25N
rows.statement: Worked example forbidding naive multiplicative LR combination (19*15=285) when both likelihood ratios derive from the same underlying document — 'directly connects 25U to 25N.'

rows.anchor: Corroboration should be measured in independent information, not number of agents ... perhaps the key result of 25U
rows.statement: States what is called 'perhaps the key result of 25U': corroboration should be measured in independent information, not number of agents.

rows.anchor: Test A three agents one source -> IndependentClusters=1 not 3 PASS. Test B three independent measurements -> IndependentClusters=3 if justified PASS. Test C same claim different contexts -> NoConflict PASS. Test D same claim same time contradictory -> Conflict PASS. Test E trusted but unauthorized -
rows.statement: Runs eight falsification tests (A-H, all PASS) against the multi-agent model: three agents citing one source yield IndependentClusters=1, not 3; three genuinely independent measurements yield IndependentClusters=3 if independence is justified; the same claim in different contexts yields NoConflict; the same claim at the same time with contradictory measurements yields Conflict; a trusted but unauthorized actor yields ReliableEvidence with Authority=False; a high-confidence LLM conclusion lacking evidence yields Unsupported; an unresolved conflict routes to Zero; and new independent evidence can update the epistemic state via ConflictResolution.

experiment.hypothesis: The multi-agent trust/conflict/consensus model behaves correctly across eight representative scenarios.
experiment.setup: Eight scenarios A-H spanning shared-source agreement, independent-measurement agreement, apparent and genuine conflict, unauthorized-trusted evidence, unsupported high-confidence LLM claims, and conflict resolution/update.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply the trust/independence/conflict rules to each scenario
experiment.result: All eight scenarios produce the theoretically expected outcome
experiment.interpretation: Confirms the model avoids conflating agent count with evidence count and trust with authority/truth.

rows.anchor: provenance graphs; dependency clusters; conflict graphs; trust statistics; ... Bayesian aggregation; consensus rules; authority checks ... EntityResolution+DependencyAnalysis+LargeGraphInference ... engineering/scaling challenges. A normal PC can execute the fundamental mechanisms
rows.statement: Lists the layer's computational primitives as normal-PC computable, with entity resolution + dependency analysis + large graph inference identified as the scaling-challenge frontier rather than a theoretical barrier.

rows.anchor:
25U — PASS ... AgentCount
eq EvidenceCount ... Consensus
eq MajorityVote ... Trust
eq Authority ... Trust
eq Truth ... Conflict
eq Failure ... IndependentEvidenceConvergence>RawAgentAgreement
rows.statement: Step 25U self-verdict: PASS, with six boxed conclusions: AgentCount≠EvidenceCount; Consensus≠MajorityVote; Trust≠Authority; Trust≠Truth; Conflict≠Failure; IndependentEvidenceConvergence>RawAgentAgreement.

rows.anchor: Identity->Observation->Evidence->Dependency->Assessment->Knowledge->Inference->Model->Prediction->Decision->Action->Observation ... Time, Context, Provenance, Authority, Trust, Uncertainty ... Zero->Lord->Information/Decision Action
rows.statement: Presents a consolidated twelve-stage architecture loop with six cross-cutting dimensions (Time, Context, Provenance, Authority, Trust, Uncertainty) and the Zero->Lord->Information/Decision-Action escape path.

rows.anchor: Approved ... technically reviewed / Architecture Board formally authorized / manager accepted the change ... The word is identical. The meaning is not ... Step 25V
rows.statement: Closes by posing the semantic-interoperability question — identical words ('Approved') carrying different meanings across bounded contexts, which perfect identity resolution and evidence aggregation cannot solve — transitioning to Step 25V (Semantics, Ontology, Bounded Contexts, Meaning Alignment, Semantic Interoperability), invoking DDD Bounded Context/Ubiquitous Language/Context Mapping/Anti-Corruption Layer as mathematically and computationally important.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Conflict(A,E_1,E_2) ... same entity? same time? same context? same proposition? same measurement? independently acquired? authoritative? different scopes? Only then can we resolve the conflict
rationale_evidence.statement: Defines Conflict(A,E1,E2) and requires an eight-question diagnostic checklist (entity, time, context, proposition, measurement, independent acquisition, authority, differing scopes) before attempting resolution.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Conflict->Identity check->Temporal check->Context check->Semantic proposition check->Dependency check->Source reliability->Authority->Independent corroboration->Resolution/Unresolved ... much safer than weighted voting
rationale_evidence.statement: Presents a nine-stage conflict-resolution pipeline, explicitly 'much safer than weighted voting.'

Byzantine consensus asks can nodes agree despite faulty nodes; KnowledgeOS asks which proposition is epistemically justified given evidence of different quality and provenance ... EvidenceQuality must remain distinct from NodeCount
rationale_evidence.statement: Explicitly distinguishes EpistemicConflict from Byzantine consensus: the problems overlap but are not identical since KnowledgeOS asks which proposition is epistemically justified, not merely whether nodes can agree — 'a truthful minority with direct evidence may be more valuable than a majority repeating weak evidence' — EvidenceQuality ≠ NodeCount.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Architect A: migration is safe / Architect B: migration is unsafe ... should not immediately calculate 50%/50% ... often disagreement is actually ModelDifference rather than FactDifference
rationale_evidence.statement: Worked human-disagreement example: two architects' conflicting risk assessments should not be treated as a 50/50 split without checking whether the disagreement is really ModelDifference rather than FactDifference.
