single_candidate_flags.why_uncertain: This file's twenty KOS-CHALMERS-001..020 entries substantially restate content already captured under chalmers-conceptual-distinction-lens's twelve KOS-EPISTEMIC-001..012 tags from S0430, applied to the same source (Chalmers' The Conscious Mind); it is unclear whether the estate intends these two numbering schemes to be merged, superseded, or kept as parallel registers from two separate extraction passes.

A ten-step variant of the eleven-step agent discipline already proposed in S0430 (IDENTIFY/EXPLICATE/SEPARATE/MODEL/TRACE/OBSERVE/BRIDGE/CHECK COHERENCE/TEST INVARIANCE/ADJUDICATE/PRESERVE GAPS); the step ordering and count differ slightly (this version merges ADJUDICATE and PRESERVE GAPS into 'STATE THE GAP' and adds 'SEPARATE LEVELS' as step 2), so it is unclear whether this is the same proposal restated or a deliberately revised version.

sources.note: S0430's extraction from Chalmers' The Conscious Mind, deliberately importing only the methodological discipline (phenomenal/psychological, explication/explanation) not the consciousness theory: 118 sections deriving DDD lessons about conceptual distinction, bridging principles, organizational invariance, functional organization, and eight new candidate models (ArchitecturalClaim/FunctionalOrganization/Realization/EquivalenceClaim/BridgingPrinciple/CoherenceAssessment/Invariant/ArchitecturalInvariant); registers a twelve-item KOS-EPISTEMIC-001..012 tag set possibly related to but distinct from shieber-epistemic-process-lens's KOS-EPI series (S0403); explicitly continues philosophy-of-complex-systems-condition-structured-knowledge-lens (S0429) into a combined condition-structured + level-structured synthesis.

rows.anchor: Do not collapse distinct concepts merely because they are correlated; first establish the conceptual distinction, then identify the functional relationship, then establish the strength of the dependency, and only then decide what can be reduced, generalized, or implemented.
rows.statement: Extraction from Chalmers' The Conscious Mind, explicitly not importing his theory of consciousness but its methodological discipline: his phenomenal (what something is like) vs psychological (what it does/causal role) distinction, and his explication (clarifying what a phenomenon/concept is, conceptual) vs explanation (how it is realized by lower-level facts, empirical) distinction, generalize to a DDD principle -- 'a domain concept, its observable behavior, its functional role, its implementation, and our knowledge of it are different things.' Core three-principle reduction: never infer semantic identity from functional similarity; never infer explanatory sufficiency from implementation correspondence; before asking how something works, make sure what is being explained has been correctly identified.

rows.anchor: Semantic Collapse ... Domain Concept -> observed behavior -> implementation -> AI-generated description -> treated as one thing
rows.statement: DDD lessons 1-2: do not conflate concepts that happen to correlate -- a named anti-pattern 'Semantic Collapse' where Domain Concept/observed behavior/implementation/AI-generated description get treated as one thing; KnowledgeOS should instead preserve Concept{has functional role, has behavioral manifestations, is realized by mechanism, is represented by artifacts, is described by observations}. Explication comes before explanation: architecture investigations often begin with 'how is this implemented?' before establishing 'what exactly is this thing?', proposing the sequence Domain Inquiry->Explication->Semantics->Function->Relationships->Implementation, and treating Concept Discovery as a distinct epistemic activity from Implementation Discovery (an agent must not conclude 'I found the code, therefore I know the domain concept').

rows.anchor: consciousness can mean subjective experience, awareness, reportability, wakefulness, cognitive access, control ... these usages identify distinct phenomena
rows.statement: Reinforces Ubiquitous Language: a familiar term (Chalmers's example: 'consciousness' covering subjective experience/awareness/reportability/wakefulness/cognitive access/control) can hide multiple distinct concepts; KnowledgeOS vocabulary must preserve distinctions (e.g. 'Decision' possibly meaning proposal/determination/approval/adjudication/command/recommendation/observed-outcome), and 'if two concepts answer different questions, they should not be merged merely because they usually co-occur.'

rows.anchor: explaining a causal role does not automatically explain the associated phenomenal property ... Same behavior ≠ same meaning
rows.statement: Third DDD lesson: functional similarity does not imply semantic identity -- Chalmers' critique of functionalism (explaining a causal role does not explain the phenomenal property) generalizes to Same behavior!=Same meaning and Same functional role!=Same domain concept; example: PaymentAuthorizationService and RiskDecisionService both producing ACCEPT/REJECT look functionally similar but are semantically completely different -- functional shape is insufficient to determine bounded-context meaning, named as an important protection against AI-generated architectural hallucination.

rows.anchor: logical supervenience ... natural supervenience ... consciousness may naturally supervene on physical properties without logically supervening on them
rows.statement: Fourth DDD lesson: relationships have strength -- Chalmers' logical supervenience (B follows from A by conceptual/logical necessity) vs natural supervenience (A sufficient for B via an actual law/regularity, not conceptually guaranteed) motivates typed dependency semantics: a bare 'A depends_on B' loses critical semantics that could be logical dependency, business invariant, causal dependency, runtime dependency, temporal dependency, deployment dependency, data dependency, policy dependency, historical dependency, or empirical correlation; proposes Dependency{source, target, relation_type, strength, conditions, evidence, rationale, validity}.

rows.anchor: reductive explanation [is] a kind of "mystery-removing" explanation rather than the only possible form of explanation ... Implementation explanation ≠ architectural explanation
rows.statement: Fifth/sixth DDD lessons: explanation is not the same as description -- a code trace (Controller->Service->Repository->Model) can fully describe implementation without answering why a capability exists, what invariant it protects, which domain concept it represents, why the boundary is there, why a dependency exists, or what business decision created it ('implementation explanation != architectural explanation'); the explanatory level must match the question (semantic/behavioral/architectural/causal/implementation/operational/governance), so an agent asked 'what does Contestation mean?' must not answer purely from a class definition but must search Ubiquitous Language, domain rules, use cases, events, tests, architecture, implementation, and governance decisions together.

rows.anchor: an epistemic lever ... The transition from evidence to claim must be explainable.
rows.statement: Seventh DDD lesson (rated one of the most valuable in the book): use bridging principles explicitly -- Chalmers observes inferring consciousness from physical observation only works via an implicit 'bridging principle' ('epistemic lever'); KnowledgeOS has such implicit bridges everywhere ('test passes'->'invariant holds', 'class exists'->'domain concept exists', 'event emitted'->'business transition occurred', 'ADR approved'->'architecture governed by decision X'); proposes making the bridge explicit via Evidence-interpreted_by->BridgingPrinciple-warrants->Claim, illustrated with a resolver-delegation example, framed as directly aligned with deterministic assurance ('the transition from evidence to claim must be explainable').

rows.anchor: explanatory coherence requirement ... different explanatory accounts should not look like unrelated coincidences; they should fit together into a unified picture
rows.statement: Eighth/ninth DDD lessons: coherence is a validation mechanism -- Evidence A + Evidence B + known relation R yielding a coherent interpretation is stronger than a single Evidence A->claim; Knowledge Claim Confidence should not be mere evidence-counting but coherence analysis across semantic/behavioral/implementation/test/governance/architectural evidence; when domain/implementation/tests/governance disagree, that should produce an Observation (semantic/behavioral/implementation incoherence detected) feeding Investigation->determine authoritative representation->adjudication->knowledge transition, rather than being silently reconciled.

rows.anchor: principle of organizational invariance ... An invariant belongs to the level at which the invariant actually holds.
rows.statement: Tenth/eleventh/twelfth DDD lessons around organizational invariance (systems sharing fine-grained functional organization should share the same higher-level property, regardless of physical substrate, taken purely as an architecture lesson not a metaphysical claim): invariants belong to the level at which they hold (Physical/Implementation/Functional/Domain/Governance invariant kept distinct -- a domain invariant like 'a determination cannot be issued without an adjudicated decision' does not imply a specific persistence implementation invariant); 'same architecture' is meaningless without specifying granularity (System-level, Behavioral, Functional equivalence are distinct); functional organization (components+states+dependency-relations+inputs+outputs+state-transitions) is more abstract than implementation topology, illustrated by two structurally different tech stacks realizing the same Command->validate->determine->persist->publish-event organization.

rows.anchor: An implementation claim requires evidence that the implementation actually realizes the claimed organization ... simulation ≠ realization
rows.statement: Thirteenth/fourteenth/fifteenth DDD lessons: architecture should preserve realizability without coupling to one realization (Domain invariant->Functional contract->Ports->multiple realizations, supporting Hexagonal/DDD); implementation must be demonstrated not merely declared ('an implementation claim requires evidence that the implementation actually realizes the claimed organization', distinguishing ArchitectureClaim from ArchitectureRealizationEvidence); simulation is not automatically realization (an AI narrating 'imagine the system works like this' does not mean the repository realizes it), requiring distinct Hypothesized/Observed/Validated Architecture states.

rows.anchor: Information can serve as a common abstraction across different realizations ... A stable abstract structure can be represented across heterogeneous realizations.
rows.statement: Sixteenth/seventeenth/eighteenth DDD lessons: Chalmers' speculative information-as-bridge metaphysics (Chapter 8, explicitly not adopted as metaphysics) is used only for the structural insight that information can serve as a common abstraction across realizations, giving Semantic Information->Functional Information->Implementation Information->Operational Information with explicit mappings; structural coherence can connect levels without collapsing them (Domain/Functional/Implementation structure coherent without being identical), supporting cross-level mapping chains (Domain Concept-realized_by->Capability-implemented_by->Application Service-observed_as->Runtime Behavior) and the idea that architectural properties can remain invariant across substrate changes (e.g. PHP->Java, MySQL->PostgreSQL).

rows.anchor: A explains structure of B without A = B ... These are not interchangeable [relation taxonomy]
rows.statement: Nineteenth/twentieth DDD lessons: coherence does not mean reduction (Implementation can explain Runtime behavior without Implementation=domain meaning; Tests can evidence a Domain invariant without Test=invariant), motivating a relation taxonomy of at least defines/realizes/implements/supports/evidences/constrains/derives/observes/explains/correlates_with/depends_on/refines, none interchangeable; claims should carry their dependency basis (Claim C depends_on {A,B,C} with dependency type logical/structural/empirical/implementation/governance), illustrated by a rule ('Operation X only possible during Voting') supported by an explicit realization chain from domain rule through resolver/middleware/tests/observed runtime.

rows.anchor: Test the architecture by constructing transformations that should preserve an invariant and see whether the claimed invariant survives.
rows.statement: Twenty-first DDD lesson: negative cases (Chalmers' absent/fading/dancing qualia thought experiments, which test whether a claimed relationship survives transformation) become a proposed 'Invariance Testing' verification method: an Architecture Invariant is run through transformation scenarios (implementation/adapter/persistence/framework/deployment substitution) to check whether the invariant survives; if not, the invariant was actually coupled to implementation rather than genuinely architectural.

experiment.hypothesis: A claimed architectural invariant genuinely holds at the domain/functional level rather than being coupled to a specific implementation.
experiment.setup: An architecture invariant (e.g. 'lifecycle authority belongs to StateMachine') and a set of implementation-substitution scenarios (middleware/controller/service/frontend/adapter/persistence/framework/deployment swaps).
experiment.assumptions: The substitution preserves the intended architecture's other properties.
experiment.inputs: The invariant statement and the transformation scenario set.
experiment.method: Apply each transformation and check whether the invariant still holds (e.g. does authority still reside in the same conceptual place).
experiment.interpretation: If the invariant survives, it has genuine architectural-level evidence; if not, it was coupled to a specific implementation.
experiment.limitations: Not run in this file; proposed as a future verification method.
experiment.conclusion: Proposed as 'Invariance Testing', an extension of the existing architecture verification approach.

rows.anchor: same API does not imply same architecture ... System A ≡ System B with respect to: X
rows.statement: Twenty-second/twenty-third DDD lessons: coarse behavioral similarity is insufficient when functional organization differs (two services with the same API and status code can be architecturally completely different), so 'same API' != 'same architecture' and 'same output' != 'same domain semantics'; equivalence claims must be scoped ('System A === System B with respect to: API behavior/domain invariants/workflow transitions/persistence semantics'), and Chalmers' own admission that coherence/organizational-invariance constrain but do not complete a theory reinforces that a constraint is not a complete architecture, and an observation does not automatically become an architecture decision -- a progression of Observation/Constraint/Principle/Hypothesis/Architecture Decision/Architecture Baseline should be kept distinct.

rows.anchor: Pattern observed repeatedly does not immediately become Kernel invariant ... fundamental psychophysical laws [vs] higher-level regularities
rows.statement: Twenty-fourth/twenty-fifth/sixty-third DDD lessons: don't promote a useful heuristic to a law -- a candidate invariant must pass Observation->Pattern->Hypothesis->Repeated evidence->Candidate invariant->Governance review->Accepted invariant, not skip stages; separate fundamental rules from derived rules (Chalmers distinguishes fundamental psychophysical laws from higher-level regularities like coherence principles, which should be consequences of deeper principles) mapping to Kernel invariant->derived governance rule->domain rule->mechanism->implementation, so a derived mechanism-level rule should not be placed directly in the Kernel -- this book is read as supporting Kernel minimalism (only sufficiently fundamental concepts, not every useful rule).

rows.anchor: Agent-generated design is not implemented architecture ... PROPOSED / OBSERVED / REALIZED-VERIFIED
rows.statement: Twenty-sixth/twenty-seventh DDD lessons for AI Engineering: agent-generated design != implemented architecture, and generated code != validated realization, motivating three distinct states PROPOSED/OBSERVED/REALIZED-VERIFIED (Proposed Architecture->Implementation->Verification->Realized Architecture); computation is useful because it describes organization, not merely symbol manipulation, so the important object is 'organization of state transitions and dependencies' rather than 'code' itself, proposing a FunctionalModel{components, states, inputs, outputs, transitions, dependencies, invariants, constraints} intermediate representation sitting between Domain Model and Implementation Model, letting an AI derive Functional Organization from implementation and a separate Domain Model from documentation/language/governance, then compare them -- 'far more rigorous than generating a C4 diagram directly from source code.'

rows.anchor: explaining cognitive functions does not automatically explain consciousness ... Explained ≠ Observed
rows.statement: Twenty-eighth/twenty-ninth/thirtieth DDD lessons: preserve the explanatory gap -- observed behavior does not automatically mean understood architecture, and passing tests do not automatically mean understanding why the architecture is correct, giving Explained!=Observed and a richer epistemic ladder (Unknown->Observed->Described->Interpreted->Modeled->Explained->Verified->Adjudicated->Established), explicitly non-linear (Observed->Hypothesized can occur without Explained, better modeled as a state machine/epistemic graph than a document status); semantic uncertainty, empirical uncertainty, implementation uncertainty, and governance uncertainty must be kept distinct types of 'unknown' (five example causes given for an agent's 'I don't know what this component does'); information structure matters, not just quantity, supporting a knowledge graph/relation-based representation over flat documents (Knowledge{concepts, relations, constraints, states, transitions, evidence, models, provenance}, with documents as representations of knowledge rather than the model itself).

rows.anchor: Representation portability must not imply semantic mutation ... bounded context is a model with a particular semantic and functional boundary
rows.statement: Thirty-first through thirty-third DDD lessons: the same semantic structure can be preserved across heterogeneous representations (Markdown/YAML/JSON/database/graph/code/diagram/AI-context) -- 'representation portability must not imply semantic mutation'; the Inverted Earth thought experiment (internal functional organization vs wider environmental properties) maps to bounded-context-vs-external-environment, reinforcing that a bounded context is 'a model with a particular semantic and functional boundary', not the whole truth about the system, and different contexts can legitimately model the same real-world phenomenon differently (illustrated by Determination/Decision/Outcome/Mandate across four contexts referring to closely connected but non-interchangeable concepts).

rows.anchor: Rule 1: Do not merge terms merely because they correlate ... Rule 5: Do not let implementation vocabulary redefine domain vocabulary.
rows.statement: Five extracted Ubiquitous Language rules: (1) do not merge terms merely because they correlate; (2) define each term according to the question it answers; (3) record synonyms only when they are genuinely synonymous in context; (4) preserve context-specific meanings; (5) do not let implementation vocabulary redefine domain vocabulary. Applied to DDD tactical elements: aggregates should be understood through state+allowed transitions+dependencies+invariants+observable behavior (not merely an entity list); domain services through responsibility+inputs+outputs+state dependencies+invariants (not a class name); events represent evidence of an observed transition without being the entire semantic definition of the concept (event!=concept, but event->evidence of state transition may be valid); state machines are functional organization models, not merely implementation utilities.

rows.anchor: a test can be understood as: Evidence that a claimed functional relation survives a specified transformation or input ... test passes should mean the tested proposition held under the tested conditions, not the architecture is correct
rows.statement: A test is defined as evidence that a claimed functional relation survives a specified transformation or input, creating a direct epistemic bridge Architecture Claim->Expected invariant->Test->Observation->Evidence; but a passing test must not be overclaimed -- it means only that the tested proposition held under the tested conditions, not that the architecture is correct. Proposes an Evidence{source, observation, proposition_tested, method, conditions, result, scope, limitations} model feeding Claim-supported_by->Evidence with an explicit support_strength and bridging_principle.

rows.anchor: ArchitecturalClaim, FunctionalOrganization, Realization, EquivalenceClaim, BridgingPrinciple, CoherenceAssessment, Invariant, ArchitecturalInvariant
rows.statement: A set of eight new candidate KnowledgeOS models is proposed with full field lists: ArchitecturalInvariant{proposition, abstraction_level, invariant_structure, realization_constraints, evidence, valid_implementations, invalidating_conditions}; ArchitecturalClaim{proposition, abstraction_level, scope, assumptions, realization, evidence, dependency_basis, invariants, invalidation_conditions, confidence, status}; FunctionalOrganization{components, states, transitions, inputs, outputs, dependencies, invariants, behavioral contracts}; Realization{abstract_target, concrete_system, mapping, preserved_properties, assumptions, evidence, verification}; EquivalenceClaim{subject_a, subject_b, equivalence_relation, abstraction_level, preserved_properties, excluded_properties, evidence, validity_conditions}; BridgingPrinciple{source_domain, target_domain, mapping, rationale, evidence_basis, assumptions, scope, known limitations}; CoherenceAssessment{claim, evidence_set, representations, expected_relationships, observed_relationships, contradictions, gaps, verdict}; Invariant{statement, semantic_level, scope, realization_constraints, supporting_evidence, verification_method, invalidation_conditions}.

rows.anchor: What should enter the Kernel? Very little.
rows.statement: Kernel-boundary recommendation: strong Kernel candidates limited to Identity, Relation, Evidence, Claim, Validity, Provenance, State, Transition, Scope (possibly Invariant if independently justified); FunctionalOrganization, BridgingPrinciple, CoherenceAssessment, Realization, EquivalenceClaim, Model, Perspective, Explanation, Simulation, Inference should remain KnowledgeOS epistemic/domain mechanisms above the Kernel, not Kernel laws -- grounded in Chalmers' own admission that his high-level coherence/organizational-invariance principles constrain but do not constitute a fundamental theory.

rows.anchor: What should NOT be adopted from Chalmers
rows.statement: Explicit non-adoption list: naturalistic dualism (a metaphysical thesis specific to consciousness, not an architectural principle); consciousness as a fundamental property (not relevant); panpsychist/information metaphysics (Chapter 8, explicitly speculative, not to be imported); strong AI as established fact (a philosophical argument from Chalmers' premises, not evidence current AI is conscious); organizational invariance as a universal engineering law (only the invariance-TESTING METHOD is extracted, not a claim that Chalmers proved architectural invariance in software).

rows.anchor: KOS-EPISTEMIC-FINDING-CHALMERS-001
rows.statement: Formal research finding KOS-EPISTEMIC-FINDING-CHALMERS-001: 'Knowledge claims should preserve the distinction between semantic concept, functional role, realization, observation, and inference; correlation or structural correspondence between these levels does not by itself establish identity or explanatory sufficiency.' Rated DDD relevance very high, Kernel relevance potentially high but not yet sufficient to change the Kernel, AI-agent relevance extremely high, architecture-verification relevance extremely high. Two candidate principles proposed: 'Semantic Authority Must Not Be Inferred From Implementation Realization Alone' (an implementation can realize a domain concept but cannot by itself define what it means) and 'every nontrivial cross-level knowledge claim must have an identifiable evidential bridge.'

rows.anchor: An implementation observation must not be promoted directly into a domain-semantic claim without an explicit semantic bridge.
rows.statement: A named anti-hallucination AI-engineering invariant: an implementation observation must not be promoted directly into a domain-semantic claim without an explicit semantic bridge -- illustrated as INVALID: seeing class ContestedOutcome and asserting 'the domain defines Contestation as X' directly, versus VALID: code observation + ubiquitous language + domain behavior + tests + governance evidence -> semantic claim. Companion invariants: a passing implementation test establishes only the tested proposition under the tested conditions, not that 'the architecture is correct'; a model must declare the level at which equivalence is claimed (e.g. equivalent with respect to domain behavior but not runtime topology/persistence/deployment); every cross-level inference should expose its bridge (test->invariant, code->domain meaning, ADR->current architecture, event->state transition, diagram->runtime topology) even when the bridge seems obvious to humans, because an AI system needs it represented explicitly.

rows.anchor: Architectural invariants should be defined independently of their current realization wherever possible. ... Coherence is evidence, not identity.
rows.statement: Two more agent-facing invariants: 'architectural invariants should be defined independently of their current realization wherever possible' -- example: 'Determination is persisted in Determination model' (realization-coupled, bad) vs 'Determination state must be durably preserved before DeterminationIssued becomes observable' (invariant-level, better); 'architecture comparison requires an explicit equivalence relation' (A~=B under a named equivalence, e.g. behavioral or domain-invariant or API-contract equivalence); and 'coherence is evidence, not identity' -- ADR/Code/Tests/Runtime all agreeing is strong evidence but they remain independent representations exhibiting coherence, not the same source, preventing the common AI mistake of treating agreeing documentation and code as literally one source.

rows.anchor: 11-step agent workflow derived from Chalmers: IDENTIFY, EXPLICATE, SEPARATE, MODEL, TRACE, OBSERVE, BRIDGE, CHECK COHERENCE, TEST INVARIANCE, ADJUDICATE, PRESERVE GAPS
rows.statement: An eleven-step agent reasoning discipline derived from the whole extraction: (1) IDENTIFY the concept/question actually at hand; (2) EXPLICATE its meaning in the bounded context; (3) SEPARATE semantic/functional/implementation aspects; (4) MODEL the claimed functional organization; (5) TRACE how it is realized; (6) OBSERVE the evidence demonstrating realization; (7) BRIDGE evidence to claim via an explicit principle; (8) CHECK COHERENCE across domain/architecture/code/tests/governance; (9) TEST INVARIANCE across relevant transformations; (10) ADJUDICATE what can legitimately be established; (11) PRESERVE GAPS -- what remains unexplained or uncertain; rated 'extremely strong agent methodology.' A companion richer Observation{observed_subject, observation_level, method, conditions, observed_behavior, interpretation, confidence} model keeps Observation/Interpretation/Claim explicitly distinct.

rows.anchor: DDD is not merely about modeling nouns and boundaries. It is about preserving distinctions between: meaning, behavior, organization, realization, observation, knowledge.
rows.statement: Final synthesis: a full DDD mapping table renders each Chalmers concept (phenomenal/psychological concept, explication/explanation, functional role/organization, supervenience, logical/natural necessity, coherence principle, bridging principle, organizational invariance, fine-grained organization, implementation, information structure, explanatory gap, thought experiment, fading/dancing qualia, strong AI, multiple concepts of mind) into a corresponding DDD/KnowledgeOS interpretation, explicitly labeled as the extraction's own inference, not Chalmers' terminology; deepest contribution stated as 'DDD is not merely about modeling nouns and boundaries. It is about preserving distinctions between meaning, behavior, organization, realization, observation, knowledge' -- since collapsing these levels creates explanatory confusion.

rows.anchor: Knowledge must be condition-structured ... Knowledge must be level-structured because concept, function, realization, observation and explanation are not the same thing.
rows.statement: Bottom-line synthesis combining this extraction with the prior complex-systems book (S0429): complex-systems philosophy taught that 'knowledge must be condition-structured because the system itself is dynamic, multi-scale and perspective-dependent'; Chalmers adds that 'knowledge must be level-structured because concept, function, realization, observation and explanation are not the same thing' -- combined into a pipeline CONCEPT-semantics->FUNCTION-organization->REALIZATION-observation->EVIDENCE-epistemic bridge->CLAIM-conditions/perspective/scope->ADJUDICATION, with the crucial DDD rule: 'do not collapse meaning, behavior, implementation, evidence and knowledge into one object. Model the relationships between them.'

lineage_claims.quote: The previous complex-systems book taught us ... Chalmers adds a different but complementary discipline

rows.anchor: A domain concept, its observable behavior, its functional role, its implementation, and our knowledge of it are different things. ... Never infer semantic identity from functional similarity.
rows.statement: Records Chalmers' first-reading constraint distinguishing a domain concept, its observable behavior, its functional role, its implementation, and our knowledge of it as different things, yielding 'never infer semantic identity from functional similarity.'
invariants: Never infer semantic identity from functional similarity.

rows.anchor: Behavioral understanding must not be promoted to semantic understanding without additional evidence. ... No high-value architectural claim without an identifiable evidential bridge.
rows.statement: Records the Chalmers re-reading's constraints: behavioral understanding must not be promoted to semantic understanding without additional evidence, and no high-value architectural claim may stand without an identifiable evidential bridge — described as the most directly applicable item of this constraint family, requiring any inference from behaviour/function/representation to identity/semantics/ontology to name an explicit bridge.
invariants: No high-value architectural claim without an identifiable evidential bridge.

rows.anchor: never infer semantic identity from functional similarity . behavioural understanding must not be promoted to semantic understanding without additional evidence . no high-value architectural claim without an identifiable evidential bridge . never infer ontology directly from representation... the corpus supplies the general rule of which v1.1's rows are cases. That generalisation is the finding.
rows.statement: Confirms a four-constraint inference-licensing family (never infer semantic identity from functional similarity; behavioural understanding must not be promoted to semantic understanding without additional evidence; no high-value architectural claim without an identifiable evidential bridge; never infer ontology directly from representation) as the general rule of which existing law rows (C-1: canonical-form equality is a similarity claim, not an identity determination; r4: probability!=truth, canonicalization!=authority, low entropy!=certainty) are specific cases -- law has the instances, the corpus supplies the rule.

lexical.anchor: Do not collapse distinct concepts merely because they are correlated; first establish the conceptual distinction, then identify the functional relationship, then establish the strength of the dependency, and only then decide what can be reduced, generalized, or implemented.

conceptual.anchor: an epistemic lever ... The transition from evidence to claim must be explainable.

formal.anchor: logical supervenience ... natural supervenience ... consciousness may naturally supervene on physical properties without logically supervening on them

operational.anchor: Test the architecture by constructing transformations that should preserve an invariant and see whether the claimed invariant survives.

governance.anchor: Pattern observed repeatedly does not immediately become Kernel invariant ... fundamental psychophysical laws [vs] higher-level regularities

rationale_evidence.anchor: explaining a causal role does not automatically explain the associated phenomenal property ... Same behavior ≠ same meaning
rationale_evidence.statement: Third DDD lesson: functional similarity does not imply semantic identity -- Chalmers' critique of functionalism (explaining a causal role does not explain the phenomenal property) generalizes to Same behavior!=Same meaning and Same functional role!=Same domain concept; example: PaymentAuthorizationService and RiskDecisionService both producing ACCEPT/REJECT look functionally similar but are semantically completely different -- functional shape is insufficient to determine bounded-context meaning, named as an important protection against AI-generated architectural hallucination.

sources.note: S0894's Step 25C.2: a fully worked numerical Bayesian likelihood-ratio experiment (0.5->0.905->0.977->0.728 across E1/E2/E3) grounding independence-vs-identity, idempotency, EvidenceCount!=EvidenceStrength, ArtifactMultiplicity!=InformationMultiplicity, non-monotonic-inference/cumulative-history, Inference-as-projection-of-KnowledgeState, a reproducible InferenceResult record, NotEveryPropositionRequiresStatisticalInference with four reasoning modes and a governed ReasoningContract, NumericalPrecision!=EpistemicValidity, A1-A10 properties, ModelPlurality, and a candidate evidence algebra E_H feeding Assessment then Inference(...); hands off to Step 25C.3 (Evidence Dependence and Information Value).

rows.anchor: When several pieces of evidence support the same proposition, how should KnowledgeOS combine them? We must avoid the very tempting but incorrect rule: more sources \Rightarrow more certainty. That is only true under specific assumptions.
rows.statement: Frames Step 25C.2's question, warning against the tempting-but-incorrect rule 'more sources ⇒ more certainty', true only under specific assumptions.

rows.anchor: Start with a controlled proposition ... H="Rollback will succeed if executed." P(H)=0.5. This is an experimental prior, not a KnowledgeOS principle. ... Evidence E_1 ... P(E_1\mid H)=0.95 and P(E_1\mid\neg H)=0.10. LR_1=9.5. O(H)=1. O(H\mid E_1)=9.5. P(H\mid E_1)\approx90.5\% under this specific sta
rows.statement: Works a fully numerical Bayesian likelihood-ratio calculation (LR1=9.5) yielding P(H|E1)≈90.5% under an explicit experimental prior, explicitly not a KnowledgeOS principle.

rows.anchor: Important observation ... We have not said "KnowledgeOS now knows rollback will succeed." We have established P(H\mid E_1)\approx0.905 under the assumptions of the model. That is statistical inference, not epistemic truth. Probability\neq KnowledgeState. This confirms the layered architecture from 2
rows.statement: Confirms via the numerical example that Probability≠KnowledgeState — a computed posterior is statistical inference under model assumptions, not epistemic truth, validating the layered architecture from 25C.1.

rows.anchor: Add genuinely independent evidence ... E_2 is an independently performed restore test. P(E_2\mid H)=0.90 and P(E_2\mid\neg H)=0.20. LR_2=4.5. Under the conditional-independence assumption LR_{12}=LR_1LR_2=42.75. P(H\mid E_1,E_2)\approx97.7\%. This demonstrates the legitimate case where independent e
rows.statement: Computes the legitimate independent-evidence-combination case: LR12=LR1·LR2=42.75 yielding P(H|E1,E2)≈97.7%, demonstrating substantial legitimate confidence increase under genuine independence.

rows.anchor: Now attack the independence assumption ... E_2 is simply a report generated from E_1. E_2=f(E_1). If we nevertheless calculate LR_{12}=LR_1LR_2, we manufacture certainty. This is mathematically wrong. IndependentEvidence must be established, not assumed.
rows.statement: Shows that applying LR1·LR2 to a copied (E2=f(E1)) evidence pair manufactures false certainty mathematically — IndependentEvidence must be established, not assumed.

rows.anchor: Perfect duplicate experiment ... E_2=E_1. Then P(H\mid E_1,E_2)=P(H\mid E_1). There should be no additional information. Aggregate(E,E)=Aggregate(E) for duplicate evidence. This confirms the idempotency requirement.
rows.statement: Numerically confirms the idempotency requirement: a perfect duplicate provides zero additional posterior shift.

rows.anchor: A surprising consequence ... the real input to inference is not \{E_1,E_2,\ldots,E_n\}. It is closer to Evidence Graph where we know relationships such as E_1\perp E_2 or E_2=f(E_1). This is not an implementation detail. It changes the mathematics of aggregation. ... Three cases ... Case A duplicate
rows.statement: States that the true input to inference is the Evidence Graph (relationships, not a bare set), classifying three information-gain cases (duplicate=0, dependent=less than naive, independent=>0) as the beginning of an evidence-combination theory.

rows.anchor: Experiment — contradictory evidence ... E_3: Rollback test failed. P(E_3\mid H)=0.05 and P(E_3\mid\neg H)=0.80. LR_3=0.0625. 42.75\times0.0625=2.671875. P(H\mid E_1,E_2,E_3)\approx0.728. So the statistical model says approximately 72.8\%. ... But KnowledgeOS must not say merely "72.8%" ... Support=\
rows.statement: Computes contradictory-evidence-adjusted posterior P(H|E1,E2,E3)≈72.8% while requiring the epistemic Support/Challenge structure be retained alongside the scalar — the critical result that the statistical result and qualitative epistemic state must coexist.

rows.anchor: The statistical result and epistemic state coexist ... EpistemicAssessment + StatisticalInference. Proposition: Rollback will succeed. Evidence: E1 supports, E2 supports, E3 challenges. Conflict: true. Statistical model: P(H|E) = 0.728. Inference model: Bayesian. Dependency assumptions: E1 ⟂ E2. Thi
rows.statement: Constructs a worked full record combining EpistemicAssessment and StatisticalInference (evidence roles, conflict flag, model, dependency assumptions), far richer than a bare confidence percentage.

rows.anchor: Experiment — source reliability ... E_3 comes from an uncalibrated test. We should not simply discard it. Instead its statistical model should represent P(E_3\mid H) and P(E_3\mid\neg H) appropriately. Reliability belongs in the model, not as an arbitrary score.
rows.statement: States that source reliability belongs inside the statistical likelihood model (P(E|H), P(E|¬H)) rather than as an arbitrary bolt-on score.

rows.anchor: Experiment — one very strong evidence item versus many weak ones ... E_1 is a direct successful restore test. Then ten weak human statements. Naive counting says 10>1. KnowledgeOS must not use source count. EvidenceCount\neq EvidenceStrength.
rows.statement: Reaffirms EvidenceCount ≠ EvidenceStrength using a strong-single-test-vs-ten-weak-statements experiment.

rows.anchor: Experiment — common-cause dependence ... Infrastructure report, Operations report, Manager report all generated from the same monitoring dashboard. E_1,E_2,E_3 are highly correlated. There are three artifacts but approximately one underlying information source. This is exactly why lineage matters. .
rows.statement: Contrasts a common-cause-dependent evidence set (three reports from one dashboard, one underlying source) with a genuinely independent evidence set (three separate physical systems), showing only the latter legitimately increases support.

rows.anchor: The crucial requirement ... KnowledgeOS therefore needs to distinguish ArtifactMultiplicity from InformationMultiplicity. Three documents can represent one underlying fact. One experiment can generate several genuinely distinct observations. This is an epistemic identity problem, not merely a databa
rows.statement: Distinguishes ArtifactMultiplicity from InformationMultiplicity as an epistemic identity problem, not merely database deduplication.

rows.anchor: Experiment — evidence arriving sequentially ... After E_1: P(H)=0.905. After E_2: P(H)=0.977. After contradictory E_3: P(H)=0.728. This demonstrates Knowledge/evidence evolution can be non-monotonic. The numerical inference can increase and decrease as evidence arrives. ... But the evidence history
rows.statement: Traces the full sequential posterior evolution (0.5→0.905→0.977→0.728), confirming non-monotonic inference alongside cumulative evidence history — InferenceState is revisable, EvidenceHistory is cumulative, matching 25A.3's earlier result.

rows.anchor: Experiment — retraction ... E_3 is later determined to be invalid. We do not erase the historical fact that at t_3, KnowledgeOS received E_3. Instead Status(E_3)=Invalid. Then recompute P(H\mid E_1,E_2,E_3^{invalid}). The inference can return toward 97.7%. But the history records why the inference c
rows.statement: Works a retraction experiment where E3 is invalidated (not erased), triggering a recomputed posterior returning toward 97.7% while the history records why.

rows.anchor: This produces an important invariant ... I_{t+1}=Infer(K_{t+1},M). If evidence is retracted K_{t+1}=Revision(K_t,E^{invalid}). Then I_{t+1} must be recalculated. Inference is a projection of KnowledgeState, not the KnowledgeState itself. This is an important architectural principle.
rows.statement: States the invariant Inference is a projection of KnowledgeState, not the KnowledgeState itself — requiring recalculation whenever the underlying KnowledgeState is revised (e.g. via retraction).

rows.anchor: This changes how we should model probabilities ... We should not store only P(H)=0.728. We should store InferenceResult=(H,Probability,Model,ModelVersion,InputKnowledgeSnapshot,Assumptions). Hypothesis: H, Probability: 0.728, Model: Bayesian, ModelVersion: 1.2, KnowledgeSnapshot: K17, Assumptions: E
rows.statement: Defines a full reproducible InferenceResult=(H,Probability,Model,ModelVersion,InputKnowledgeSnapshot,Assumptions) record instead of storing a bare probability.

rows.anchor: This is extremely important for KnowledgeOS ... Why did KnowledgeOS say rollback had a 72.8% probability? We should be able to answer Because K_{17} + Model_{1.2} + Assumptions_{X} \Rightarrow0.728. This is much stronger than "The AI estimated 72.8%."
rows.statement: Argues the InferenceResult record enables answering 'why did KnowledgeOS say 72.8%?' with a precise reconstruction (snapshot+model+assumptions), far stronger than 'the AI estimated it'.

rows.anchor: We now have a candidate inference contract ... Inference(K,H,M,C) \rightarrow R where K = knowledge snapshot; H = hypothesis; M = mathematical model; C = assumptions/context; R = inference result. This is a clean DDD/application boundary.
rows.statement: Defines the inference contract Inference(K,H,M,C)→R as a clean DDD/application boundary.

rows.anchor: What should happen if the model is inappropriate? ... Architecture Board approval is mandatory. Trying to calculate P(ApprovalRequired) is usually the wrong operation. The appropriate reasoning may be RuleEvaluation(K,Policy) \rightarrow Required. NotEveryPropositionRequiresStatisticalInference. Thi
rows.statement: Argues NotEveryPropositionRequiresStatisticalInference (a normative approval requirement should use RuleEvaluation, not probability), reinforcing the rejection of a universal Bayesian kernel, and defines four reasoning modes (Deductive/Normative, Statistical, Causal, Semantic/Fuzzy).

rows.anchor: The reasoning engine itself therefore becomes governed ... ReasoningContract which specifies Question type, Applicable model, Required evidence, Assumptions, Output semantics, Acceptable uncertainty. This prevents an LLM from casually selecting whatever reasoning mechanism produces the desired answe
rows.statement: Defines a governed ReasoningContract (six fields) preventing an LLM from casually selecting whichever reasoning mechanism produces its desired answer.

rows.anchor: A particularly dangerous failure ... There is a 92% chance the migration will succeed. KnowledgeOS should ask: Where did 92% come from? There must be Model + Inputs + Assumptions + Calculation. If none exist, 92% is merely an unsupported assertion. NumericalPrecision\neq EpistemicValidity. ... This
rows.statement: States NumericalPrecision ≠ EpistemicValidity: an LLM-stated percentage with no model/inputs/assumptions/calculation is merely an unsupported assertion, requiring semantic provenance on every generated number or it remains CandidateInference.

rows.anchor: What has 25C.2 actually established? A1 Duplicate idempotency E\oplus E=E. A2 Independent evidence can accumulate E_1\perp E_2 \Rightarrow Information(E_1,E_2)>Information(E_1) under suitable conditions. A3 Dependent evidence must not be double-counted. A4 Contradiction must remain visible. A5 Infer
rows.statement: Consolidates ten properties A1-A10 established by Step 25C.2: duplicate idempotency, independent accumulation (conditional), non-double-counting of dependent evidence, visible contradiction, model/assumption/snapshot-dependence of inference, recomputation on retraction, invalid unmodeled numerical output, and not-all-questions-are-statistical.

rows.anchor: Our first candidate KnowledgeOS evidence algebra ... \mathcal E_H=(Support_H,Challenge_H,Unknown_H,Dependency_H,Temporal_H,Provenance_H) ... Assessment_H = A(\mathcal E_H,C) ... Inference_H = M(Assessment_H,K_t,C) where M is an explicit reasoning model.
rows.statement: Consolidates the candidate evidence algebra E_H=(Support,Challenge,Unknown,Dependency,Temporal,Provenance)_H feeding Assessment_H=A(E_H,C) then Inference_H=M(Assessment_H,K_t,C) under an explicit model M.

rows.anchor: The architecture now becomes very clean ... Evidence ↓ Evidence Graph ↓ Epistemic Assessment ├──► Rule Engine ├──► Statistical Engine ├──► Causal Engine ├──► Logical Engine └──► Semantic/Fuzzy Engine ↓ Inference ↓ Decision. The kernel does not care which inference mathematics is used, as long as the
rows.statement: Diagrams the clean five-engine architecture (Rule/Statistical/Causal/Logical/Semantic-Fuzzy) all feeding a common Inference→Decision path, with the kernel agnostic to which mathematics is used as long as the contract is explicit.

rows.anchor: One more mathematical attack: order of evidence ... For genuinely independent evidence under the same model: Infer(E_1,E_2)=Infer(E_2,E_1). But sequential world events are different: Event_1\rightarrow Event_2 may not equal Event_2\rightarrow Event_1. So we must distinguish EvidenceAggregation from
rows.statement: Distinguishes commutative EvidenceAggregation from order-sensitive WorldEventComposition — another reason the temporal model must remain separate from the evidence-aggregation algebra.

rows.anchor: Another attack: conflicting priors ... P_1(H)=0.5 and P_2(H)=0.9. They receive identical evidence. They can produce different posterior probabilities. Therefore a probability is not simply a property of the evidence. It is Inference(E,Model,Prior,Assumptions). This must be recorded. ... Consequence
rows.statement: Shows two different priors on identical evidence legitimately produce different posteriors, requiring KnowledgeOS preserve multiple parallel inference results (ModelPlurality) rather than treat one as universal truth.

rows.anchor: The next major concept ... When should KnowledgeOS trust one inference model over another? That is not merely evidence aggregation. It is ModelSelection. normative question → rule engine; measurable stochastic phenomenon → statistical model; causal intervention question → causal model; vague linguis
rows.statement: Identifies ModelSelection (choosing which reasoning engine applies to which question type) as a distinct next problem, essential to Zero/Lord/Sārathi.

rows.anchor: 25C.2 Verdict ... PASS with an important qualification: Bayesian mathematics works very well as a specialized inference engine, but only after KnowledgeOS has modeled evidence dependency, provenance, temporal scope and assumptions. It should not become the epistemic kernel itself.
rows.statement: Verdicts Step 25C.2 PASS with the qualification that Bayesian mathematics is an excellent specialized inference engine only after dependency/provenance/temporal-scope/assumptions are modeled — never the epistemic kernel itself.

rows.anchor: Current mathematical architecture ... KnowledgeOS = EpistemicKernel + EvidenceGraph + InferenceEngines + DecisionMathematics with EpistemicKernel: Evidence + Assertion + Assessment + Conflict + TemporalValidity + Provenance + Revision. Then InferenceEngine: (\mathcal A,M,C) \rightarrow InferenceResu
rows.statement: Consolidates the current architecture KnowledgeOS=EpistemicKernel+EvidenceGraph+InferenceEngines+DecisionMathematics with each layer's concrete inputs/outputs specified.

rows.anchor: The next experiment ... Step 25C.3 — Evidence Dependence and Information Value. How much new information does E_2 provide given E_1? This naturally leads to I(E_2;H\mid E_1) — conditional information. And potentially VOI(a) for Lord's epistemic actions. We can test whether independent evidence reall
rows.statement: Proposes Step 25C.3 (Evidence Dependence and Information Value): formalize conditional information I(E2;H|E1) and connect to VOI(a), aiming for a mathematically rigorous bridge Evidence→Information→Investigation→Zero/Lord.

single_candidate_flags.why_uncertain: S0403 (shieber-epistemic-process-lens) also uses a 'KOS-EPI-01..10' numbering convention for its own distinct invariant register; this file's 'KOS-EPISTEMIC-001..012' tags are a different, self-declared register from Chalmers, not shown to be identical to S0403's KOS-EPI series, but the near-identical naming convention (KOS-EPI vs KOS-EPISTEMIC) raises a genuine identity question worth flagging.

sources.note: S0403's external epistemic lens applying Shieber's epistemology textbook to KnowledgeOS: separates claim from state-of-affairs, evidence from truth, requires a basing relation, distinguishes coherentism/foundationalism/externalism, and proposes a seven-concept kernel model (KnowledgeClaim/Evidence/Grounding/Derivation/Source/Lineage/KnowledgeAssessment) plus ten KOS-EPI invariants; distinct from the generic 'evidence' Operational Evidence Register object and from knowledgeos-kernel-concept (B0005).

rows.anchor: Shieber explicitly separates: know-how; knowledge-wh; knowledge-that
rows.statement: Shieber's epistemology distinguishes know-how, knowledge-wh (who/what/where/when/why), and knowledge-that (propositional/factual knowledge); DDD implication: 'Knowledge' should not be used as the universal object for everything, and the central object should be called 'Knowledge Claim' rather than simply 'Knowledge'.

rows.anchor: A Knowledge Claim is not the reality it describes.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-01 Claim/Reality Separation: a claim is an assertion about a state of affairs, not the state of affairs itself; kernel pipeline proposed as World/System State -> Observation -> Claim -> Assessment -> Knowledge Status, explicitly not Document -> Truth nor AI output -> Knowledge.

rows.anchor: Evidence does not constitute truth.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-02 Evidence/Truth Separation: evidence supporting a claim does not itself constitute truth; someone can arrive at a true belief via poor evidence, or hold excellent evidence while being wrong. Therefore Evidence != Truth != Claim != Knowledge Status.

rows.anchor: He calls this the basing relation.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-03 Basing: it is insufficient merely to possess good evidence -- the belief/claim must actually be based on that evidence (the 'basing relation'), modeled as a semantic Evidence -BASIS_FOR-> Claim relationship rather than a bare claim.evidenceIds[] array. Example given: Observation 'Service A calls Service B' + runtime-trace Evidence != mere reference; the claim must be BASED ON that evidence.

rows.anchor: Evidence should have domain identity and provenance.
rows.statement: Proposed Evidence structure: EvidenceId, Source, Observation/Artifact reference, CapturedAt, Context, EvidenceKind; and a Claim.EvidenceBasis relation carrying evidence, role, and basis rationale as first-class, meaningful fields.

rows.anchor: Coherence increases epistemic support but does not establish truth by itself.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-05 Coherence Is Not Truth: coherentism (mutually supporting web of beliefs rather than a foundational hierarchy) is useful for the knowledge graph (supports/explains/constrains/consistent-with/contradicts/depends-on edges) but a perfectly coherent set of beliefs can still fail to correspond to objective reality.

rows.anchor: the coherence is generated by one lineage
rows.statement: AI hallucination graph rule: if Claude generates a chain A->B->C->D and then a review claiming they are 'mutually consistent,' this must not be treated as four independent confirmations because the coherence is generated by one lineage; the kernel must preserve Epistemic Lineage and distinguish Independent Support from Derived Support.

rows.anchor: Every derivation chain should be traceable to one or more originating grounds.
rows.statement: Foundationalism (hierarchical structure where some beliefs serve as foundations for others) motivates supporting 'Foundational Evidence' / 'Primary Ground': every derivation chain should be traceable to one or more originating grounds (e.g. Runtime Observation -> Architecture Claim -> Derived Design Interpretation), without making KnowledgeOS a foundationalist system.

rows.anchor: The kernel should not commit philosophically to either foundationalism or coherentism.
rows.statement: The kernel must be graph-shaped, not tree-shaped: it should support both foundationalist grounding chains and coherentist mutual-support webs, via a KnowledgeGraph carrying grounding edges, derivation edges, support edges, contradiction edges, contextual edges, provenance edges, and temporal edges, representing domain relationships rather than committing to either philosophical theory.

rows.anchor: the classic stopped-clock example
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-04 Process Matters: externalism says what matters is not merely evidence a knower can inspect but whether the belief-producing process is reliably accurate; the stopped-clock example shows TRUE + EVIDENCE + BASING is still insufficient without PROCESS RELIABILITY as a separate concern, mapped to the Verification/Assurance Engine.

rows.anchor: Epistemic Grounding ... from ... Process Assurance
rows.statement: Distinguish Epistemic Grounding ('why do we believe this?') from Process Assurance ('why should we trust the process that produced this?'), illustrated by a 'Build is reproducible' claim example with separate Evidence (three successful builds), Process (deterministic verification procedure), and Assurance (reproducibility gate passed) fields.

rows.anchor: The kernel therefore needs Assessment, not just Evidence
rows.statement: Proposed KnowledgeAssessment concept evaluating a claim against Evidence, Grounding, Derivation, Source, Process, Context, Contradictions, and Temporal validity, producing Claim -> Assessment -> Epistemic Status rather than Claim -> isKnowledge=true.

rows.anchor: Persistence of a claim is not proof of persistence of its validity.
rows.statement: Memory is a preservative source of knowledge but is also subject to confabulation/false-memory distortion over time; therefore persistence of a claim is not proof of persistence of its validity -- a claim created at T1 may be valid at T1, challenged at T2, superseded at T3, with the historical record retained, reinforcing temporal determinism, replay, historical state, supersession, and evidence lineage work already underway.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS externalizes epistemic memory.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-07 Historical Evidence Must Survive Forgetting: a person can retain a justified belief even after losing the original evidence/reasoning; a KnowledgeOS claim must not become unjustified merely because the human or agent no longer remembers the reasoning -- the claim's historical basis (observation, evidence, reasoning, verification) must survive independently of the current agent's memory ('KnowledgeOS externalizes epistemic memory').

rows.anchor: Provenance cannot depend on the agent remembering provenance.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-06 Provenance Must Be Externalized: humans are poor at remembering the sources of their beliefs (source-monitoring failures), so provenance must be systemically captured -- automatic, immutable, machine-readable, queryable -- rather than depending on an agent recalling 'where did you get this.'

rows.anchor: Agent output is testimony/proposal until independently established by the KnowledgeOS assurance process.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-08 Source Reliability Is a Process Property: externalist testimony accounts require the testimony be connected to a reliably accurate process, yet humans are poor at monitoring testimony reliability; therefore AI agent output should flow AI Agent -> Testimony/Proposal -> Evidence -> Verification -> Assessment -> Accepted Knowledge, never directly AI Agent -> Knowledge.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS should model epistemic processes, not merely epistemic documents.
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-09 Distributed Cognition Requires System-Level Provenance: modern scientific knowledge is increasingly produced by socially distributed cognitive processes divided across people, tools, computers, and organizations (closely matching the AI Engineering Platform's Human/AI Agent/KnowledgeOS/Repository/Verification/Governance/Board/CI-CD/Runtime chain); therefore KnowledgeOS should model epistemic processes, not merely epistemic documents, and the AI Engineering Platform and KnowledgeOS should be distinct but cooperating bounded contexts.

rows.anchor: Local understanding of a process is not equivalent to system-level understanding of the process.
rows.statement: Distributed cognition introduces a domain risk: participants may not know why the overall process succeeds, and two people in the same activity can interpret it differently, so 'local understanding of a process is not equivalent to system-level understanding of the process' -- Agent Context != Platform Context != Knowledge Context != Governance Context, supporting bounded contexts rather than a universal AI 'context.'

rows.anchor: 5 agents repeat the same claim does not necessarily equal 5 independent sources
rows.statement: KOS-EPI-10 Independent Support Requires Lineage Awareness: social networks can propagate information reliably but popularity/network structure can influence acceptance; five agents repeating the same claim (Agent A->B->C->D->E) is one lineage, not five independent sources, so the kernel needs Evidence Independence / Source Lineage to prevent AI echo chambers.

rows.anchor: Source ... Lineage ... should therefore be distinct
rows.statement: Source ('where did this information originate?') and Lineage ('through which transformations and actors did it reach us?') should be modeled as distinct concepts; a final claim may have many contributors (e.g. Runtime -> Observation -> Human -> Claude -> Architecture Proposal -> Reviewer -> KnowledgeOS) but only one primary empirical source.

rows.anchor: Declarative Knowledge ... Procedural Knowledge ... Operational Know-How
rows.statement: Someone can perform reliably without being able to articulate how they do it (performative vs acquaintance know-how); this implies KnowledgeOS should eventually distinguish Declarative Knowledge, Procedural Knowledge, and Operational Know-How, without putting executable procedures into the same aggregate as claims -- suggesting a further split of Knowledge into Assertions vs Practices/Procedures.

rows.anchor: perception does not provide an unmediated copy of reality
rows.statement: Perception involves a process between the world and beliefs (not an unmediated copy of reality), reinforcing the existing Observation != Reality model: World -> Observation mechanism -> Observation -> Interpretation -> Claim; an observation is not 'the truth,' so Observation must remain a first-class domain object.

rows.anchor: Was this result generated by a process that is itself trustworthy for this class of claim?
rows.statement: Deterministic assurance should verify the process, not just the answer, since a result can accidentally be correct; an Assurance Record should carry Subject, Method, Inputs, Preconditions, Execution, Result, Environment, Version, and Timestamp, and the epistemic question becomes whether the generating process is itself trustworthy for that class of claim.

rows.anchor: I see approximately seven kernel concepts.
rows.statement: Proposed seven-concept KnowledgeOS Kernel candidate model: KnowledgeClaim (ClaimId/Content/Context/Lifecycle/Status), Evidence (EvidenceId/Kind/ContentReference/CapturedAt/SourceRef), Grounding (the basing relation, Evidence->Claim), Derivation (Inputs/Method/Output/Conditions, incorporating the Audi extraction on inference/transmission), Source (Identity/Type/Provenance/Qualification), Lineage (Source->Evidence->Claim->Derivation->Claim path), and KnowledgeAssessment (Evidence basis/Derivation/Process assurance/Contradictions/Context/Temporal validity/Decision) -- all situated under cross-cutting Context, Time, Identity.

lineage_claims.quote: This incorporates our Audi extraction around inference/transmission.

rows.anchor: EpistemicStatus should NOT be a boolean
rows.statement: EpistemicStatus must not be modeled as a boolean isKnowledge flag; proposed enum-like states Proposed/Supported/Assessed/Accepted/Challenged/Defeated/Superseded/Reinstated are offered, but even that may be too simplistic since status has multiple dimensions (e.g. evidentially strong, operationally verified, governance accepted, temporally obsolete simultaneously) -- so EpistemicStatus is kept as a domain concept under investigation, not a frozen enum.

rows.anchor: What I would not put into the kernel yet
rows.statement: DDD tells us to keep the kernel small and semantically powerful: explicitly excludes from the kernel ConfidenceScore, TruthScore, a universal ReliabilityScore, a philosophical Foundationalism aggregate, a philosophical Coherentism aggregate, Belief as the primary domain object, Mind, Consciousness, SubjectiveExperience, generic Trust, generic AIKnowledge, and a universal KnowledgeGraph aggregate -- classifying these as analytical lenses, policies, or infrastructure concerns rather than kernel domain objects.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS is not fundamentally a repository of knowledge.
rows.statement: Deeper DDD conclusion: rather than KnowledgeOS = Knowledge + Evidence + Governance + AI, the stronger domain model is an EPISTEMIC PROCESS pipeline (Observe/Communicate/Reason -> Evidence -> Ground/Derive -> Claim -> Assessment -> Assurance & Governance -> Knowledge Status -> KnowledgeOS); KnowledgeOS is not fundamentally a repository of knowledge but an epistemic infrastructure for producing, grounding, assessing, preserving, challenging, and governing engineering knowledge -- a much stronger DDD bounded-context boundary.

rows.anchor: Putting Audi + Williamson + Shieber + our existing DDD/assurance/governance work together
rows.statement: Combined kernel diagram integrating Audi + Williamson + Shieber: Context -> Knowledge Claim -> {Grounding -> Evidence -> Source -> Provenance -> Temporal Validity; Derivation -> Lineage/Process-Method; Assessment -> Epistemic Status}, with Observation, Assurance, Governance, Review, AI Engineering, Retrieval, Workflow, and Knowledge Delivery placed outside the kernel as the KnowledgeOS Platform; conclusion: 'Knowledge is produced by processes, grounded in evidence, transmitted through relations, distributed across systems, preserved through time, and assessed under conditions' is the level at which the KnowledgeOS domain kernel should operate.

rationale_evidence.statement: The kernel must be graph-shaped, not tree-shaped: it should support both foundationalist grounding chains and coherentist mutual-support webs, via a KnowledgeGraph carrying grounding edges, derivation edges, support edges, contradiction edges, contextual edges, provenance edges, and temporal edges, representing domain relationships rather than committing to either philosophical theory.
